verses.1:
Al-Mizan explains barāʾa as recoiling from, disassociating oneself from, or becoming free of something detested; its cognates can express freedom from illness, disavowal of a person, absolution, or innocence. The verse is a heading that succinctly announces the subject developed in the following passage, like the opening summary of an independent sūrah.

The plural in ilā alladhīna ʿāhadtum shows that the address is either to the faithful or to the Prophet together with them. Allah is the source of the proclamation, the Messenger conveys it, and the polytheists are its object; the Prophet and believers are to communicate it to those absent. Such a public mode of proclamation also manifests the grandeur of its issuer.

The repudiation is a decree, but not a merely legislative one, since the Messenger is joined to Allah in issuing it; purely legislative rule is assigned to Allah, as in and none shares with Him in His ruling (18:26). It announces the withdrawal of security from treaty-bound idolaters, not an arbitrary cancellation. Most had proved untrustworthy by violating the treaty in practice, and repudiation was permitted where treachery was feared: And if you fear treachery from a people, break offwith them in a like manner. Surely Allah does not like the treacherous (8:58). Yet the other side had to be notified, lest cancelling the treaty take them unawares and itself become forbidden khiyāna.

The later exception for those who neither violated the treaty nor aided others against the Muslims—barring the polytheists with whom you have made a treaty, and who did not violate any with you, nor backed anyone against you. So fulfil the treaty with them until its term. Indeed Allah loves the Godwary (9:4)—confirms that repudiation was justified by breach. Even violators received a period of grace so that they would not be surprised. Thus the treaty and its security cease for those whose violations, or expected future treachery and harm, made them unreliable.
verses.2:
Al-Mizan notes that siyāḥa means travel or movement upon the earth, as sāʾiḥ describes flowing water. The command to travel for four months is not literal: it grants the idolaters four months of immunity from aggression, in which they may choose the course they judge best between survival and destruction. The warning that they cannot thwart Allah urges them to abandon polytheism for monotheism rather than arrogantly bring disgrace upon themselves. Directly addressing them, after speaking of them in the third person, conveys decisiveness, Muslim superiority, and contempt for their power to retaliate.

The context indicates that the period begins on the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage, when the repudiation was proclaimed, so that they receive their full grace period from the day of notification. Since the verses were revealed in 9 A.H., and this day is taken to be yawm al-naḥr, the 10th of Dhū l-Ḥijja, the period comprises the final twenty days of Dhū l-Ḥijja, Muḥarram, Ṣafar, Rabīʿ al-Awwal, and the first ten days of Rabīʿ al-Thānī.

Other commentators begin it on the 20th of Dhū al-Qaʿda, which they identify as the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage, yielding its final ten days, Dhū al-Ḥijja, Muḥarram, Ṣafar, and twenty days of Rabīʿ al-Awwal. Others date revelation to 1st Shawwāl and identify the four months with Shawwāl, Dhū al-Qaʿda, Dhū al-Ḥijja, and Muḥarram, treating Then, when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists (9:5) as the pre-Islamic Sacred Months. Al-Mizan rejects this latter reading as wholly unsupported by the context.
verses.3:
Al-Mizan explains adhān as notification. Although this verse and A repudiation by Allah and His M essenger… (9:1) both declare repudiation, they differ in delivery. The first both proclaims it and addresses the treaty-bound idolaters; this verse announces it to the Muslim public, so that they may prepare to carry out the commands concerning the idolaters after the sacred months. This is indicated by an announcement… to the people and its sequel: Then, when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them… (9:5).

The commentary holds that the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage (Yawm al-Ḥajj al-Akbar) was the day of slaughtering the sacrificial animals in 9 A.H. Traditions from the Prophet’s Household support this, and it best suits a proclamation made when Muslim and polytheist pilgrims were gathered in Minā. Sunnī collections also report this identification, though most make the day of slaughter the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage in every year, for which the traditions provide no basis. Identifying it with the Day of ʿArafa, because standing at ʿArafa distinguishes the Greater from the Lesser Pilgrimage, is unsupported ratiocination; identifying it with the following day, when the Muslim leader is said to preach, is plainly weak. Nor does the context support taking it to mean the whole Ḥajj period: a particular day on which all pilgrims assembled provided the natural occasion for the proclamation, and the expression would accordingly call that day to mind rather than days without such an assembly.

The renewed direct address to the idolaters—that they cannot thwart Allah—continues the admonition of (9:2). If you repent that is better for you makes explicit that this warning counsels them not to remain idolaters and bring themselves to perdition. Finally, the address shifts to the Prophet in and give news to the faithless of a painful punishment, since the warning must be delivered to its recipients directly.
verses.4:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse exempts treaty partners who neither violated their agreement directly nor supported others against the Muslims indirectly. Muslims are therefore obliged to fulfil such treaties to their full term. Direct breach includes such acts as killing Muslims; indirect breach includes military assistance to their enemies. The Meccan idolaters’ arming of Banū Bakr against the Prophet’s ally Khuzāʿa, despite the Treaty of Ḥudaybiyya, exemplified the latter and was among the causes of the Muslim conquest of Mecca in 8 A.H.

Indeed Allah loves the Godwary makes treaty-keeping a part of general Godwariness (taqwā), not merely caution against unjustified treaty-breaking. In Qur’anic usage, taqwā means avoiding all that Allah has forbidden, and no contextual indication narrows muttaqīn here to those wary only of violating a treaty.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan identifies “the sacred months” here with the four-month period of safe movement granted to the polytheists in the preceding proclamation, not with the pre-Islamic calendar’s sacred months. The definite expression refers back to months already designated for that grace period, and the timing of the proclamation does not align with an alternative calendar-based reading. When those allotted months have elapsed, the repudiation becomes effective and the prior guarantee of protection ends.

The command to kill the polytheists “wherever” they are found is interpreted as universal in both place and time, including sacred places and months. Its stated purpose is to expose the polytheists to destruction after the respite, gradually cleanse the earth of them, and spare people from mixing and associating with them. The sequence names the available means according to circumstance: if Muslims can reach and kill them, they are to do so; otherwise they are to capture them, contain them by siege, or wait in ambush where their location is uncertain. The lexical senses of siege and ambush reinforce this progression from direct seizure to containment and concealed waiting.

Al-Mizan rejects the suggestion that the verse simply offers an unrestricted choice between killing on one side and capture, siege, and ambush collectively on the other. That construction strains the wording, whereas the context presents several practical methods for carrying out one policy. It likewise rejects rearranging the verse to mean “seize them wherever you find them and kill them,” because neither the passage nor its continuation supplies grounds for reversing the stated order. The resulting interpretation is severe and explicit: once the announced grace period has expired, the polytheists covered by the repudiation may be pursued by whatever available method brings the campaign to completion.

The continuation places a decisive limit on that ordinance. If they repent, maintain prayer, and give zakāt, their way must be cleared and aggression against them must cease. Here repentance bears its lexical sense of returning: they turn from idolatry to monotheistic faith and demonstrate that return through prayer, zakāt, and adherence to the religious duties owed to their Creator. “Let them alone” evokes travellers whose blocked road is opened so that they may proceed unmolested.

God’s being all-forgiving and all-merciful most naturally explains why He commands that they be released: He forgives and shows mercy to those who return to Him. A second possible reading makes the Muslims’ act of letting them go an expression of those divine attributes which they should emulate, but the first reading better accords with the apparent wording.
verses.6:
Al-Mizan reads this verse as a necessary qualification of the repudiation and revocation of security: any idolater seeking asylum in order to hear the Word of Allah must be granted it, even if he belongs to a people with no treaty whose security has been repudiated. Promises and threats, treaties and their repudiation, and even warfare serve the Prophetic mission of turning people from error and ignorance to guidance and monotheistic felicity. Since repudiation aims to uphold truth and destroy falsehood, a person in whom guidance remains possible must not be turned away.

The asylum is granted so that the seeker may learn the true religion, have ignorance removed, and be convinced by the truth. If he nevertheless obstinately persists in error, he again falls among those whose security has been revoked. Having heard the Word of Allah, however, he must be conveyed to a place where he is safe from Muslim attack, so that he has complete safety and can choose freely after clear evidence has been presented. The provision rests on their ignorance: one who does not know is not blameworthy while guidance remains possible. The commentary calls this ordinance perhaps the highest embodiment of the morality, dignity, mercy, kindness, and respect for humanity demanded by Islam.

This verse restricts the general command to kill the polytheists wherever you find them (9:5). Safety is limited to what is needed for a religious purpose: hearing the Word of Allah, discerning guidance from error, and learning the Prophet’s teachings. It does not require safety for one seeking it without a religious aim or benefit to religion; in that case the preceding command to use force remains operative.

The Word of Allah encompasses all Qur’anic verses, while the context especially concerns verses that establish the religion’s fundamental doctrines, explain its core teachings, and answer the seeker’s doubts. Restricting it to monotheism verses, to Sūrah al-Tawba, or to verses proclaimed during the Hajj season is arbitrary. Until he hears the Word of Allah means acquaintance with those doctrines and teachings; for an Arab it may mean hearing and understanding God’s actual speech, while for a non-Arab who does not understand Arabic it means understanding the religion.

Al-Mizan declares the verse muḥkam and incapable of abrogation. It expresses the Qur’anic and Prophetic principle that punishment or harshness cannot precede incontrovertible proof, and that an ignorant seeker of truth must not be rejected. It therefore rejects the claim that Fight all the polytheists, just as they fight you all (9:36) abrogates it. The explicit command to convey the seeker to safety further shows that guidance must remain open and that people must be free to choose salvation or destruction after proof, leaving them no argument against Allah on the Day of Judgement.

Finally, citing some scholars, the commentary infers that the religion’s fundamental doctrines require definitive knowledge (ʿilm yaqīnī), not even strong conjecture (ẓann rājiḥ). If taqlīd sufficed, seekers could simply be ordered to follow Islam without investigation. Certainty may arise through rational deduction or any other means of knowledge, including coincidentally; reason is a valid means to certainty, but not its sole means.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan explains that this verse, together with those following it, clarifies both the repudiation of treaties with untrustworthy idolaters and the exemption for those who kept their agreements. How shall the polytheists have any treaty with Allah and His Messenger? is a rhetorical denial of any such treaty, except for those who concluded one at the Holy Mosque and remained steadfast in it. Muslims must remain steadfast with them so long as they remain steadfast.

Keeping peace with those who keep peace, and honouring the steadfast, are aspects of Godwariness (taqwā); hence, Indeed Allah loves the Godwary. The exception does not qualify the principle arbitrarily, but rests on the treaty partners’ having neither violated its terms nor slackened in fulfilling their pledges.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan explains ill as a manifest bond arising from an oath or pact, and dhimma as a pledge whose breach brings blame. Their juxtaposition means that, if the idolaters gained power, they would observe none of their obligations toward the faithful, whether founded on kinship or on pledged treaties and oaths.

The repeated How? continues the preceding question: How shall the polytheists have any treaty with Allah and His Messenger, when, if they overcome you, they will respect neither kinship nor covenant? They please you with their mouths means that their words outwardly please, though their hearts reject what those words profess.

This outward flattery and inward hostility explain the repudiation of their treaty. Most are fāsiqūn in that they have already violated their treaties in practice, even before gaining mastery over the Muslims. Thus, both individually and collectively, they already disregard kinship and covenant; no such regard should be expected from them if they prevail.
verses.9:
Al-Mizan explains that their selling Allah’s signs for a paltry gain and barring people from His way accounts for the preceding description of most of them as transgressors and prepares for the statement that they observe toward believers neither kinship nor covenant. Their transgression there most likely means treaty-breaking and disregard of pledges, though they also disobey Allah.

The conclusion, and it is they who are the transgressors, answers any thought that repudiating their treaty wronged them: their concealed enmity and hatred, manifested in obstructing Allah’s way and disregarding both kinship and covenant with believers, make them the aggressors.

verses.11:
Al-Mizan reads these verses as elaborating the earlier choice: If you repent that is better for you; but if you turn your backs know that you cannot thwart Allah (9:3). Repentance means returning to faith in Allah and His signs. Maintaining prayer, the clearest manifestation of worship, and giving zakāt, the backbone of religious society, represent the religious duties through which that faith is completed.

Those who do so become brethren in faith: they possess the same rights and duties as every other Muslim. This brotherhood is not a mere metaphor. It is a genuine religious kinship, recognized in Islamic law and carrying real rational and religious implications, analogous to familial kinship. As the Prophet said: ‘The believers are brothers, the lowest of them are looked after by all of them, and they are as a single fist against all others.’

The people who break their pledges after making a treaty and revile the religion are not the earlier idolaters already described as treaty-breakers; otherwise the condition of breaking pledges would be needlessly repeated. They are others who made treaties and pledges with the Muslim leader and later violated them. They are called the leaders of unfaith (āʾimmat al-kufr) because they lead in denying Allah’s signs and others follow them. Muslims are commanded to fight them and revoke their oaths, perhaps so that they will desist from violating treaties and pledges.

verses.13:
Al-Mizan explains that this verse and the next four urge the faithful to fight by recounting the idolaters’ offences: breaking their pledges, resolving to expel the Messenger, and initiating hostilities, along with their violations of truth and honesty. True faith in Allah, in whose hand are benefit and harm, requires fearing Him rather than them; this is meant to strengthen the believers and give them courage.

The verses further show that Allah tests their devotion. They must sever their ties with the idolaters in order to receive the reward of those who have attained genuine faith.
verses.14:
Al-Mizan explains that the command to fight is repeated after the preceding encouragement because believers are now mentally and spiritually prepared to receive a command that was initially new and unexpected. The stated consequences—Allah punishing and humiliating the idolaters through the believers’ hands, granting believers victory, healing faithful hearts, and removing their rage—intensify the command and rouse believers to act. In fighting, the believers are Allah’s implements in this world; the promise both denigrates the idolaters and assures believers of divine aid.

And Allah turns clemently to whomever He wishes qualifies the command, lest fighting be pursued indiscriminately.

verses.16:
Al-Mizan presents this verse as a further reason to obey the command to fight. The world is an abode of trial: souls attain nearness to Allah through struggle and sacrifice for faith in Him and His signs, and genuine faith becomes manifest only in action. Through trials, Allah distinguishes the virtuous from the vicious and those truly faithful from those who merely profess faith.

Those who claim to have sold their lives and property to Allah for paradise must therefore be tested on the battlefield, so that the truthful are distinguished from the dishonest, and those who wholly disown Allah’s enemies from those who retain loyalty and affection for them. Allah grants life to the former and causes the latter to perish. The faithful must hasten and compete in obeying the command to fight, demonstrating the truth of their faith and purity of heart before their Lord.

Do you suppose that you will be let offmeans: do you expect to remain as you are before the reality of your profession of faith has appeared? Allah has not yet ascertained means that they have not yet objectively demonstrated striving and disowning every confidant besides Allah, His Messenger, and the faithful. It does not imply divine ignorance: as in Do you suppose that you would enter paradise, while Allah has not yet ascertained those of you who have strived and not ascertained the steadfast? (3:142), Allah’s acquiring knowledge refers to the thing’s realization in objective reality. Allah is well aware of what you do confirms this. Walīja means a person one relies upon who is not a family member.
verses.17:
Al-Mizan explains that ʿamāra means preserving and repairing a structure, rather than visiting it on pilgrimage. A masjid is a place of prostration; here, “Allah’s mosques” includes every place dedicated to His worship, though the immediate case is the Holy Sanctuary, as also suggested by the alternate singular recitation. The plural does not limit the rule to Mecca, since its rationale applies to all mosques.

“It is not for the polytheists” denies them a right they never possessed to maintain, renovate, or visit such places. Their witnessing to their own unfaith means openly manifesting disbelief, whether verbally or through idolatrous worship. Thus, idolaters may not repair the Holy Sanctuary or any other mosque while they attest to disbelief by word or deed.

Their works have failed because deeds of worship are meant to attain God’s pleasure and paradise, whereas futile deeds cannot produce that end. Their remaining in the Fire confirms that such acts will not bring happiness or eternal bliss, but everlasting misery. The verse also indicates that every permissible act—whether obligatory, recommended, or legally neutral—benefits its doer, since divine law is not arbitrary; and that an act is permissible because God has granted its performer the right to do it and has not prohibited it.
verses.18:
Al-Mizan holds that innamā restricts the legal right to maintain God’s mosques exclusively to those described in the verse. Though phrased declaratively, the statement legislates permission: only those who believe in God and the Last Day may maintain them. Idolaters are excluded, for their association of partners and denial of the Last Day prevent their belief from qualifying them.

Prayer and zakāt are added because the passage concerns those whose deeds benefit them. Whoever abandons the practical requirements of religion, especially these two indispensable pillars, has disbelieved in God’s signs and gains no benefit from a verbal profession of belief in God and the Last Day, even if he still calls himself Muslim; verbal denial of Islamic teachings makes him an unbeliever outright. “Fear no one except Allah” means exclusive worship of God: religious khashya is worship, unlike instinctive fear, because worship arises from fear of a deity’s wrath or loss of its mercy.

The hope that such people will be “among the guided” does not belong to God, for hope presupposes ignorance of the future. It belongs to those described or to the hearers. Genuine belief confirmed by worship is certainly guidance, but it is hoped that guidance will become a settled and enduring quality rather than an occasional state. Accordingly, Al-Mizan concludes that no non-Muslim has the right to maintain God’s mosques: idolaters lack true belief, and the Qur’an does not recognize the belief of the People of the Book as genuine belief.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan explains siqāya here as giving water to Hajj pilgrims, a pre-Islamic office of prestige associated in historical reports with ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. Rather than supplying an implicit comparison between the people who performed this service and a believer who strives in God’s way, the commentary reads the verse through its stated conditions. Providing water and maintaining the Holy Mosque are mentioned without any condition of faith, whereas striving is expressly joined to belief in God and the Last Day.

The verse therefore repudiates the equation of outwardly similar acts performed without faith—such as pre-Islamic service to pilgrims and the Mosque—with deeds made living by faith, such as striving in God’s way. The coda, “and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing lot,” indicates that the wrongdoing is the idolatrous belief accompanying the former deeds, not merely the error of treating the two classes of deed as equal. Such works bring no guidance to eternal happiness, success, mercy, divine satisfaction, or paradise.

Those making the comparison appear to have been believers, comparing either acts they had done before conversion or acts then done by idolaters with the deeds of sincere believers. The omission of the performers of the former services may preserve the dignity of believers who did them and prevent their being identified with the wrongdoers. Al-Mizan further infers from the following verse that both groups were Meccans: those characterized by faith and striving emigrated, while the others converted but did not emigrate. A reported occasion of revelation accords with this reading: ʿAbbās boasted of supplying pilgrims with water, Shayba of maintaining the Mosque, and ʿAlī answered that he had believed in God and striven in His way.

The lasting worth of works thus depends on faith and dedication, not their outward form. The commentary adds that faith without works is like a body without an animating spirit: it has no life or value in the scale of deeds. Believers must therefore judge deeds by whether faith gives them life, not merely by their visible form.
verses.20:
Al-Mizan explains that those who believe, emigrate, and strive in God’s way with their possessions and persons have the greater rank with God; the plural wording makes these qualities, rather than particular persons, the criterion. Their superiority is not a matter of occupying one rank above people who possess a lesser rank through deeds devoid of faith. Such deeds have no merit at all before God.

Thus, “a greater rank” subtly compares the highest standing with no standing whatsoever, showing that the two groups are not truly comparable. “It is they who are the triumphant” further confines enduring and established triumph to those who believe, emigrate, and strive.
verses.21:
Al-Mizan reads these glad tidings as an explanation of the triumph granted to those who believed, emigrated, and strived in God’s way. Their Lord promises them an indescribably magnificent mercy and satisfaction, and gardens containing bliss that neither fades nor ends; they will remain there without limit or expiration.

The promise is deliberately astonishing, since it announces blessings beyond anything seen in this world and thus difficult for human minds to conceive. “With Allah indeed is a great reward” resolves this apparent incredibility: such a reward is with God.

verses.23:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse generally forbids believers from taking faithless people as allies, even when they are close kin. Fathers and brothers are singled out because taking someone as a walī means allowing that person to involve himself in one’s affairs. They are especially able to influence believers, interfere in their concerns, and turn their hearts away from actions harmful to the faithless or displeasing to them; wives and children would not normally have the same influence except through an intermediary.

The warning calls those who take such allies “the wrongdoers,” rather than merely saying that they are “from them,” since kinship might weaken the deterrent force of the warning. Its emphatic form indicates that wrongdoing becomes an established trait in them, not merely an isolated act. Since God does not guide wrongdoers, they are deprived of divine guidance: their good deeds will not secure everlasting happiness, triumph, or success.
verses.24:
Al-Mizan sees the shift from addressing the believers to addressing the Prophet as an indication that he should turn away from people whose attachment to their faithless fathers and brothers has made admonition ineffective. Their love of kin, wealth, trade, and dwellings—sources of familial and social security—keeps them from obeying God and His Messenger and from striving in God’s way, even against disbelieving relatives.

The conditional warning means that reliance on faithless relatives and preference for worldly attachments over God, His Messenger, and striving in His way will make them turn from the divine summons and forget religion’s purpose. “Then wait until Allah issues His edict” may initially signify either a divine act that repairs the harm their defection causes to the religion or a punishment for their disobedience. The coda, “Allah does not guide the transgressing lot,” shows that by such conduct they leave divine servanthood, become transgressors against God and His Messenger, and lose both guidance in their deeds and the grace of supporting the true faith and eradicating idolatry.

The commentary concludes that God’s edict is His action to support the religion: He will bring a people who love Him alone, refuse friendship with His enemies, and uphold and strive for the religion of truth. Those who fail will gain no benefit from religion, and their deeds will not be guided to truth or eternal happiness. Al-Mizan rejects the interpretation that the edict means the conquest of Mecca, since the verse addresses believers, particularly Emigrants, who themselves participated in that conquest.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan explains that mawāṭin, plural of mawṭin, literally denotes places of residence, but here refers to the many battles in which God aided the Muslims, including Badr, Uḥud, the Trench, and Khaybar. The verse and those following it recall the exceptional divine aid at Ḥunayn, the valley between Mecca and Ṭāʾif where the Muslims initially retreated before God aided them to victory. Iʿjāb means being pleased by an unusual occurrence; raḥab denotes expanse and ḍayyiq its opposite.

The commentary rejects the view that these verses conclude the Prophet’s speech in (9:24). “Allah has certainly helped you” naturally begins a new subject, and the events of Ḥunayn—divine composure, unseen hosts, punishment of the faithless, and possible forgiveness—are independently important. Had this been part of an address the Prophet was commanded to deliver, it would have required the imperative qul. Its tone, shifts of address, and rhetorical structure likewise do not fit that reading. Although the Muslims included hypocrites, weak believers, and sincere believers, the verse addresses them collectively as one Islamic community, as its reference to their impressive number shows.

“The day of Ḥunayn” means the day of battle in that valley, following the Arabic convention of naming momentous events by their place, participants, or event. Their numbers impressed them because they imagined numerical superiority could secure victory without dependence on God. Yet numbers are only an apparent cause (sabab ẓāhirī), ineffective unless God wills; He is the Cause of Causes. Thus their multitude proved useless precisely because they relied on it and forgot reliance upon God.

That “the earth became narrow” evokes their being hemmed in by enemies and unable to find shelter, not merely an inability to escape, as some commentators claim. Their turning their backs means that they fled from the front line. This was the major sin of fleeing battle, incurred through confidence in numbers and abandonment of trust in God; neither panic nor confusion falls under the stated exceptions to the prohibition on flight. Their apparent advantages consequently failed them. Nevertheless, in mercy God aided them with composure and unseen armies, punished the disbelievers, and left forgiveness possible. By neither guaranteeing forgiveness nor closing its possibility, He educates them through a balance of fear and hope.

Al-Mizan rejects an attempt to excuse the flight as an involuntary withdrawal caused by the sudden Hawāzin and Thaqīf attack. That reading relies on narrations, on the Muslims’ later return at the calls of the Prophet and ʿAbbās b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, and on Qur’anic praises of the Companions. But it confuses tafsīr, which seeks the meaning of revelation, with kalām, which defends theological positions through reason, scripture, Sunna, or consensus. Interpretive theories must not be imposed on the Qur’an. The phrase “whereupon you turned your backs” includes their conduct under the prohibition of flight; God did not limit that prohibition to cowardly or treacherous flight, exempt flight in panic, or make its exception for tactical manoeuvre or rejoining another troop applicable to them. Their later return does not alter this.

The commentary also rejects the claim that the Prophet himself lost composure, even if his alleged distress is described as grief rather than fear. Grief over a divinely decreed reversal or over the Muslims’ punishment for their own error would not accord with the Prophet’s divinely taught station, and reports do not show that he left his position or became distressed. If he grieved for the Muslims out of mercy over their error and flight, that grief was praiseworthy and would not be removed by sakīna. In any case, the later sending down of composure does not imply that he had lacked it: he remained under clear divine guidance throughout his mission.

Sakīna is not merely ordinary calmness, dignity, courage, or battlefield steadiness, since such qualities may be found in believers and disbelievers alike. Qur’anic sakīna is a distinctive divine state, sent down especially from God, by which the servant does not forget the station of his Lord. It presupposes a heart fit to receive it—truthful, sincere, and faithful to its pledge—and it increases faith, makes one adhere to the word of Godwariness, and purifies one from disobedience and sin. Thus it is more than ʿadāla, and it cannot simply have descended upon every combatant who later rejoined the battle, including hypocrites, the weak of faith, and people with sickness in their hearts.

Accordingly, “the faithful” upon whom composure was sent at Ḥunayn does not include hypocrites, those with diseased hearts, or the weak of faith. It could refer either to those who never left the Prophet or also to those who fled and later returned. But those who fled committed a major sin and could receive sakīna only after sincere regret, repentance, and return; perhaps thumma (“then”) suggests this sequence. Even this possibility is problematic, because the following verse mentions repentance and forgiveness after the sakīna, and because it would obscure the extraordinary steadfastness of the few who remained beside the Prophet while most fled. The Qur’an habitually distinguishes and praises the innocent or steadfast minority when reproving a group, as in its treatment of Uḥud and the Trench.

Al-Mizan therefore concludes that the faithful granted sakīna were the believers who stood firm with the Prophet. Those who fled and later returned may be among those to whom God subsequently turns clemently, together with guided disbelievers from Hawāzin and Thaqīf, reformed ṭulaqāʾ, and others with sickness in their hearts who reformed themselves. The differing narrations about the small number who stood firm do not alter this exegetical conclusion.

Finally, Qur’anic praise of the Companions and promises to them are conditional upon the continuing presence of faith (īmān), devotion (ikhlāṣ), veracity (ṣidq), sincerity (naṣīḥa), and striving. If these qualities disappear through wrongdoing, the praise and promises no longer apply. God’s riḍā at the Pledge of Ḥudaybiyya is a divine attribute of action (ṣifa fiʿliyya), identical here with the purity of the servant’s soul and the consequent worthiness for reward; it is not an immutable attribute of the divine essence. Should conduct deteriorate, divine satisfaction becomes anger (sukhuṭ), and blessings become misfortunes. No one has an unconditional pledge of perpetual happiness regardless of obedience, sin, faith, or disbelief.
verses.26:
Al-Mizan explains that sakīna is a state of the heart that brings tranquillity of soul and steadfastness of heart. Qur’anic passages connect it with an increase of faith and with kalimat al-taqwā, which makes a person wary of what God has forbidden or made sacred.

Sakīna differs from ʿadāla, a psychological disposition that restrains one from major sins and habitual minor sins while allowing occasional minor sins without its loss. Sakīna, by contrast, prevents every sin, major and minor. The Qur’an exclusively associates it with God, as it does rūḥ, and describes God as “sending down” (inzāl) it; it is therefore a divine gift possessed by Him and bestowed on selected persons. The verse, It is He who sent down composure into the hearts of the faithful that they might enhance their faith. To Allah belong the hosts of the heavens and the earth… (48:4), also indicates that it is among His divine hosts (junūd).

The Qur’an repeatedly joins sakīna with unseen hosts, including at Ḥunayn and in (9:40). From the context, these hosts appear to be angels, or some of them, sent to the battlefield. Sakīna and the angels support and strengthen the faithful and punish the faithless. Further aspects of this divine composure are discussed in the commentary on bearing tranquillity (sakīna) from your Lord (2:248).
verses.27:
Al-Mizan explains that when tawba is attributed to God, it means that He turns to His servant first by granting grace and success in repentance, and then by forgiveness and clemency. When tawba comes from the servant, it means turning to the Lord in regret and repentance; God does not turn to one who has not first turned to Him.

“After that” refers to the Muslims’ reliance on something other than God, their sinful flight, God’s sending down of composure and hosts, and His punishment of the disbelievers. “Whomever He wishes” therefore includes both Muslims and disbelievers: the latter must renounce disbelief, while the former must repent of their error and sin. The verse gives no basis for restricting clemency to either group.

The commentary consequently rejects the claim that the verse concerns only disbelievers punished in this world and then guided to Islam. Its clemency is general and unqualified. The verse declares that repentance, grace, clemency, and forgiveness remain continually open to all people, unlike the preceding mention of sakīna, which indicates an exclusive gift granted only to a few.
verses.28:
Al-Mizan explains that najas means impurity or dirt, while ʿayla means poverty or need. The command that polytheists not approach the Holy Mosque instructs the faithful to prevent their entry. Their najas implies an impurity belonging to them and a corresponding purity of the Holy Mosque, but it does not establish a ruling requiring avoidance of physical contact with them when moisture is present.

“After this year” refers to 9 A.H., when ʿAlī proclaimed repudiation: people were forbidden to circumambulate the House naked, and idolaters were forbidden to perform the Hajj thereafter. The assurance against poverty addresses the fear that enforcing this ordinance would deprive Mecca and those trading during the Hajj season of pilgrims, commerce, and livelihood. God promises to enrich them from His grace, if He wishes.

The promise reassured Meccans and others dependent on the Hajj markets, and its glad tidings continue for Muslims. Islam’s word and renown spread, whereas the idolaters’ way of life was being destroyed. Apart from Arabs whose treaty with the Prophet at the Holy Mosque still had time remaining, they received only four months’ grace after the repudiation proclamation and were entering Islam.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan holds that the People of the Book here are the Jews, Christians, and Zoroastrians; the Sabaeans are described as a Jewish-influenced Zoroastrian sect. The min in “from among those who were given the Book” is explanatory (bayān), not partitive (tabʿīḍ): the three descriptions apply to the People of the Book as whole communities, not merely to a subgroup among them. Had the command concerned only some of them, further clarification would have been required.

The first description, their not believing in Allah or the Last Day, does not deny that they profess belief in the Creator, scripture, and Resurrection. Rather, the Qur’an treats belief in God, the Last Day, and all His messengers as inseparable. Since they reject Muḥammad’s prophethood, they are thereby disbelievers, just as an idolater’s acknowledgement of a supreme deity does not constitute true belief in God. Their doctrines concerning Jesus or Ezra as God’s son, the Jews’ expectation of only a brief punishment, and the Christians’ belief that Christ’s sacrifice removes their sins show that their affirmation of God and Resurrection does not accord with the truths of monotheism and the Hereafter.

Their not forbidding what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden includes permitting acts prohibited in Islam, such as wine, swine’s flesh, and wrongful appropriation of wealth. “Messenger” could mean Moses and Jesus, whose prohibitions their communities disregard; but the singular wording more likely refers to Muḥammad, whose mission their own scriptures foretell. Thus the verse reproves their refusal to respect the limits set by Allah and His Messenger. Its purpose is not to require them to adopt Islamic prohibitions internally while remaining in their own religion. It is to prevent the public, unrestrained spread within Islamic society of acts Islam forbids, such as drinking wine, eating swine’s flesh, and embezzling wealth. By entering dhimma, they may retain a monotheistic religion but may not openly oppose Islam or publicly propagate such practices.

The commentary says that fighting until jizya is paid was not ordained for Muslim luxury or worldly gain. Its purpose is the ascendancy of truth, justice, and piety over falsehood, tyranny, and immorality; it safeguards moral formation and social order while allowing those who do not accept Islam to choose Judaism, Christianity, or Zoroastrianism, provided that they do not openly oppose Islam. Jizya is a monetary payment in return for protected status and for the state’s provision for their security and needs.

“Religion of truth” (dīn al-ḥaqq) means not merely a religion described as true, but the religion belonging to and leading to truth. Islam’s teachings are rooted in the realities of creation and correspond to the human fiṭra. Submission to God’s moral will (al-irādā al-tashrīʿiyya) follows from submission to His cosmic will (al-irāda al-takwīniyya); whereas truth leads to a fitting way of life, falsehood follows desire and would dissolve the order of the heavens and earth. The three descriptions therefore explain and motivate the command to fight: the People of the Book have not accepted faith acceptable to God, do not prevent publicly harmful sins, and do not follow the way of life harmonious with fiṭra and cosmic reality.

Jizya is most reliably understood as payment for safety and legal protection, not simply a penalty for unbelief. Ṣāghirūn means that they submit to the Islamic way of life and its just religious government: they do not compete for precedence in that society or advance doctrines and practices judged harmful to it. Their payment symbolizes this subordinate position, but the verse does not authorize Muslims or state agents to humiliate or mock them, which the commentary considers beneath Islam’s dignity. “Out of hand” (ʿan yad) may mean payment directly from their hand, or payment owing to Muslim authority, without their obstinacy or arrogance. Thus they are fought until they submit to that authority and pay a tribute used for their security, safety, and affairs.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan explains yuḍāhiʾūn as imitation and yuʾfakūn as being diverted from the proper course of truth into falsehood. It recounts that Ezra, or ʿUzayr, restored the Torah for the Israelites after its loss and their captivity, so that his exceptional service led them to call him “the Son of God.” It is uncertain whether this meant a share in divinity, emanation from God, identity with Him, or merely honorific veneration like the claim, “we are Allah’s sons and His beloved ones” (5:18). The following verse appears to support the latter meaning.

The claim about Ezra may have been made only by some Jews in the Prophet’s time, but the Qur’an attributes it to them generally because others tacitly approved and shared the same orientation. Christ’s sonship, by contrast, is presented as a Christian doctrine.

The commentary understands the verse to say that calling Christ God’s son, as well as the doctrine of the Trinity, imitates earlier polytheistic religions that imagined divine fathers, mothers, spouses, sons, and daughters. It further maintains that polytheistic beliefs entered Judaism and Christianity, and cites modern studies as finding close Buddhist and Hindu influences in the Tanakh and New Testament, including New Testament stories and parables. The closing words, “May Allah assail them,” are a prayer against them.
verses.31:
Al-Mizan explains aḥbār as Jewish scholars and ruhbān as Christian ascetics. Taking scribes and monks as lords besides Allah means obeying them unquestioningly, although only God deserves such obedience. Taking Christ, Mary’s son, as a lord means ascribing divinity to him; calling him Mary’s son emphasizes that he is a human being born of a woman.

The verse distinguishes this lordship from that ascribed to scribes and monks. It likewise distinguishes Ezra’s sonship from Christ’s: Ezra’s is honorary sonship (bunuwwa tashrīfiyya), while Christ’s is meant in a more literal sense. Ezra could be regarded as a lord only insofar as this followed from calling him God’s son, or because, as a scribe, he had rendered an incomparable service by restoring the Jewish faith. Christ’s alleged sonship is of a wholly different kind, since Christians make him a lord besides God.

The clause that they were commanded to worship only one Allah means that they took these lords despite that command. Absolute, unconditional obedience to someone is itself worship: one obeyed in this way as a lord is effectively treated as a god (ilāh). The verse’s use of “worship only one Allah,” rather than “take only one lord,” shows that worship is not confined to conventional ritual; it includes obedience (ṭāʿa). Accordingly, the Qur’anic command to worship God alone also requires restricting ultimate obedience to Him.

Nor is worshipping one god sufficient for monotheism if one still acknowledges other gods. True submission requires dedicating both worship and obedience to the one God, with no partner. “Immaculate is He above the partners that they ascribe” rejects both the lordship they grant to their scholars and monks and the divine partnership they ascribe to Jesus. In this way, the verse explains why taking gods besides Allah is incompatible with genuine belief in Allah and the Last Day, when sovereignty belongs to Him alone.
verses.32: Al-Mizan explains yuṭfiʾū as extinguishing a light or flame, while bi afwāhihim means using their mouths as the means of attempting it. The image compares the faithless people’s denials of Muḥammad’s prophethood to blowing at a lamp in an attempt to extinguish a light that fills the horizon and which Allah intends to bring to complete brilliance. It belittles the weakness of their effort, since a mouth can affect only a feeble light, and promises that Allah will perfect His light despite their aversion.
verses.33:
Al-Mizan identifies hudā as the divine guidance sent with Muḥammad in clear signs and manifest proofs, and dīn al-ḥaqq as Islam, whose teachings and laws correspond to objective reality and human fiṭra. God sent His Messenger with this guidance and religion so that the religion itself may prevail over every other religion, despite the polytheists’ aversion. The pronoun in “that He may make it prevail” refers to the religion of truth, not to the Messenger; the alternative interpretation, that it means making the Prophet victorious and teaching him the religion, is judged extremely unlikely.

Together with the preceding verse, this passage encourages the faithful to fight the People of the Book and presents that fighting as a religious duty. Since God wills His light to be completed and the religion of truth to spread among all people, this requires exertion and struggle against those seeking to extinguish it. They are to be fought until they are destroyed or hasten to pay tribute and submit. Muslims therefore should neither weaken nor grieve, for God wills their triumph over their enemies if they are truly believers.
verses.34:
Al-Mizan reads this verse as explaining the final two descriptions of the People of the Book in (9:29). The wrongful consumption of people’s wealth by many scribes and monks illustrates their failure to forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, while their barring others from Allah’s way explains their failure to practise the religion of truth. Monetary wrongdoing is singled out because economic order is a foundation of social stability. Extreme poverty can lead to theft, violence, fraud, and usurpation, while extreme wealth can lead to extravagance, domination by desire, and violation of others’ lives, property, and dignity. When lawful ownership and consumption collapse, society is reduced to the pursuit of appetite rather than wisdom, education, morality, or public order.

The wrongdoing is especially grave in religious leaders, whose duty is to educate and reform their communities. The commentary considers the apparent meaning to be that they accept judicial bribes; even if it referred only to the sale of indulgences, that would suffice for the condemnation. Donations, endowments, bequests, or gifts given because of apparent piety are not, in themselves, wrongful consumption, and usury and illicit earning are elsewhere attributed to the People of the Book generally rather than specifically to their clergy. Once such leaders abandon truth for falsehood, the commentary says that the livelihoods and benefits they obtain in that state are ill-gotten by reason and religion. By their powers and resources, open and hidden, they bar people from Allah’s way and thwart the moral reform and natural happiness (saʿāda) sought by the just religious government.

Kanz means hoarding gold and silver: keeping wealth from circulating through transactions in ways that benefit individuals and society. Although the verse follows criticism of the People of the Book, its wording does not confine its warning to them; Muslims too are threatened with painful punishment if they hoard wealth and do not spend it in the way of Allah. What makes hoarding blameworthy is withholding wealth when an occasion for spending it in Allah’s way exists. Sabīl Allāh includes whatever sustains the religion’s security and stability: jihād, protection of its essential interests, indispensable social affairs, and religious dues that strengthen the community. Thus those who keep gold and silver while urgent communal needs remain unmet prefer themselves and anticipated future needs to God and the present needs of religious society.

The verse does not set a maximum amount of property one may own. A person may possess much gold and silver without committing this prohibition if the wealth is used in trade, investment, employment, or other productive activity that benefits its owner and others. Such wealth is not concealed or kept from circulation, and the ruler may direct its owner to spend when a religious need arises. The prohibition concerns wealth hoarded while its owner avoids the religious dues owed from it, including obligatory taxes and urgent needs such as defending the community or saving lives. Recommended (mustaḥabb) spending, such as further support for dependants or the poor, is also spending in Allah’s way, but failure to undertake it when no necessary expenditure is due is not the forbidden kanz meant here. The threat of “a painful punishment” establishes the severity of the prohibition.

Al-Mizan explains (9:35) as the punishment promised to hoarders: their treasure will be heated in hellfire and pressed against their foreheads, sides, and backs, while they are told, “This is what you treasured up for yourselves! So taste what you have treasured!” Their wealth thus becomes their punishment in the Hereafter. The particular limbs may be symbolic: their foreheads signify abasement for wealth, their sides the shelter sought in it, and their backs the reliance placed upon it.

verses.36:
Al-Mizan understands the twelve months “with Allah” to be the lunar months of the earthly lunar year, known directly from the moon’s successive phases. Years, months, and weeks arose from observable natural cycles; although the solar year does not exactly equal twelve lunar months and requires leap reckoning, lunar months remain directly accessible to all people. The familiar system of days, weeks, months, and years is calibrated to the inhabited temperate regions of the earth, while conditions near the poles and the cycles of other planets differ. Solar months, unlike the solar year and seasons, are conventional; the twelve months grounded in observable reality are lunar.

This reading is confirmed by the four sacred months, which are lunar: Dhū al-Qaʿda, Dhū al-Ḥijja, Muḥarram, and Rajab. Further, “with God” (ʿind Allāh) and “months in God’s Book” (fī kitāb Allāh) denote an unalterable number, fixed in divine knowledge and in the Book of Creation from the creation of the heavens and earth, with the ordered courses of the sun and moon. Thus Allah’s Book here is not the Qur’an or a physical written book, as some commentators claim, but the created order that objectively establishes twelve months.

The commentary explains that ḥurum is the plural of ḥarām, meaning forbidden or inviolable, and that qayyim denotes what promotes people’s welfare and orders their affairs. According to definitive narrations, the four named lunar months are sacred, and the statement has legislative force: their sanctity is part of the upright religion. Allah made them sacred so that fighting would cease, people could enjoy security and peace, and they could turn to their Lord in worship and veneration. Their sanctity came from Abraham’s religion and was retained even by idolatrous Arabs, though they sometimes transferred a month’s sanctity through nasīʾ.

“So do not wrong yourselves during them” refers to the four sacred months, not the preceding twelve. As al-Farrāʾ noted, the pronoun fīhinna suits the four, whereas referring to all twelve would make the injunction equivalent to a perpetual prohibition with no apparent connection to the preceding statement. The command therefore particularly magnifies these months’ sanctity: it prohibits every sin and wrongdoing, while its context chiefly concerns fighting during them.

On “Fight all (kāffatan) the polytheists, just as they fight you all (kāffatan),” Al-Mizan notes proposals that kāffatan means mutual repelling or collective fighting. Grammatically, each occurrence can be connected to either Muslims or idolaters, but the most immediate reading connects each to its adjacent subject: Muslims are commanded to fight all the polytheists just as the polytheists fight all Muslims. The command consequently concerns the whole body of idol worshippers and is akin to “kill the polytheists wherever you find them (9:5)”; whatever abrogates, specifies, or restricts that verse does the same here. It concerns idolaters, not the People of the Book: although the Qur’an may attribute shirk to the latter, it reserves mushrikīn for idol worshippers. Hence this command neither abrogates nor qualifies the ruling to take tribute (jizya) from the People of the Book (see 9:29).

Finally, Allah’s being with the Godwary both promises divine aid and victory and urges Godwariness in warfare. It also restrains Muslims from exceeding Allah’s limits by killing women, children, or persons who offer greetings of peace.
verses.37:
Al-Mizan explains nasīʾ as postponing the inviolability of a sacred month: pre-Islamic Arabs delayed its prohibition on fighting until a later ordinary month rather than abolishing it. Although accounts differ over its precise operation, the verse indicates that they retained the inherited Abrahamic tradition of four sacred months while moving a month’s sanctity for a year or more, then restoring it to its proper place. This was an increase in unfaith (ziyāda fī al-kufr), for after associating idols with Allah they further interfered with His legislated ordinance.

The wrongdoing prohibited in the sacred months chiefly includes fighting. Accordingly, nasīʾ appears to mean postponing a month’s sanctity in order to fight in it, not postponing the Hajj pilgrimage. The Arabs’ life of raids and warfare perhaps made three consecutive months without fighting difficult. They would therefore move Muḥarram’s ban on fighting to Ṣafar, permitting warfare in Muḥarram while treating Ṣafar as sacred, and later return the ban to Muḥarram. Reports that they shifted the Hajj from Dhū al-Ḥijja to another month find no support in the wording of the verse.

“Whereby the faithless are led astray” indicates that others led them through this practice and implies an authority who determined when nasīʾ would occur; traditions say this authority was a member of Banū Kināna. The pronoun in “They declare it permissible in one year and forbid it another year” refers to the sacred month: in one year they permitted fighting in it by transferring its prohibition elsewhere, and in the next they again forbade fighting by restoring the prohibition to its original month. Their aim was to preserve the numerical total of four inviolable months while changing which months were protected, so that their wars and raids could continue.

The commentary identifies the one who made their evil action appear decorous as Satan. Though such an act may be attributed to Allah in the sense of recompense, evil is not attributed to Him except in that sense. When a servant sins and Allah withholds guidance, Satan gains an opening to make the sin seem attractive, corrupting and misleading the sinner. Thus the sequence—evil deeds made decorous, followed by Allah’s refusal to guide the faithless—answers how this misguidance can occur: they are disbelievers, and Allah does not guide the faithless lot.
verses.38:
Al-Mizan explains that iththāqaltum ilā al-ʿarḍ means inclining toward the ground as though burdened down. To go forth in Allah’s way is to struggle against Islam’s enemies. The believers are sharply reproached for hesitating when the Prophet summons them, as though satisfied with this worldly life in place of the Hereafter.

The construction of “Are you pleased with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?” implies that worldly life is only an inferior portion or imitation of the life to come; hence its possessions are insignificant by comparison. The Prophet’s name is omitted in the verse to magnify his rank. The verse and those following it sternly warn the believers, and may concern the campaign to Tabūk, as reported among its occasions of revelation (asbāb al-nuzūl).
verses.39:
Al-Mizan holds that the threatened painful punishment is left unspecified and should not be restricted to the Hereafter; the context suggests punishment in this world, or in both worlds. If they refuse to go forth, Allah can replace them with another people who do not shrink from His commands or from striving in His way.

Their refusal cannot harm Allah, for He has no need of them. Obedience benefits them alone, and disobedience harms them alone. Allah’s power over all things explains both His ability to punish them and to replace them.
verses.40:
Al-Mizan explains thānī al-ithnayn as “one of the two,” and ghār as a wide opening in a mountain. The cave is that of Jabal Thawr near Minā, not the Cave of Ḥirāʾ. Definitive reports identify the Prophet’s companion as Abū Bakr. The Prophet reassured him not to grieve or fear their estrangement, lack of helpers, and the enemies’ pursuit, because Allah was with them and would aid them.

The commentary maintains that “Then Allah sent down His composure upon him, and strengthened him with hosts you did not see” refers to the Prophet, not Abū Bakr. The surrounding pronouns all refer to the Prophet: the believers fail to help him, the faithless expel him, he speaks to his companion, and Allah strengthens him. No proof warrants making the one pronoun in “upon him” refer instead to Abū Bakr.

More fundamentally, the verse recounts Allah’s direct aid to His Messenger when no human being could protect or assist him. Its three occurrences of idh (“when”) progressively explain this aid: his expulsion by the faithless, his being one of two in the cave, and his speech to his companion. The descent of sakīna and the unseen hosts therefore belong to the special divine assistance granted to the Prophet. The final outcome—Allah lowering the word of the faithless and raising His own word—explains the whole account as the triumph of Allah’s aid to His Messenger.

Thus, when the Meccan idolaters pursued the Prophet to kill him, he left Mecca with only Abū Bakr. Allah then sent composure upon the Prophet, supported him with unseen hosts that turned the pursuers away, frustrated the unbelievers’ plan to kill him, and made supreme His promise to help His Messenger, make the religion triumphant, and complete His light. Allah does this as the Almighty and Wise.

The phrase “Then Allah sent down His composure” follows the general statement that Allah had already helped the Prophet, rather than being an immediate consequence of his saying, “Do not grieve.” It may also follow the whole preceding description of the time of divine aid, but it cannot thereby be assigned to Abū Bakr. The claim that the Prophet always possessed composure and so must not be its recipient is rejected: the Qur’an also describes composure as sent down upon the Messenger on other occasions, without stating that he had first become fearful or grieved. Divine bestowal need not presuppose a preceding opposite state.

Likewise, “and strengthened him with hosts you did not see” stands in the same context as the descent of composure. To assign the composure to Abū Bakr either requires assigning the unseen hosts to him as well or arbitrarily separating the two clauses. Some commentators do assign both to Abū Bakr, arguing that unseen hosts sent to believers would ultimately support the Prophet; but Al-Mizan finds this reading incoherent. It interrupts a verse whose beginning, context, and end demonstrate that Allah Himself aided the Prophet independently of believers who had been censured for failing to respond to his summons. It also turns the detailed explanation of Allah’s aid to the Prophet into an account of aid given to someone else.

The unseen hosts aided him at the time of the cave; claims that they refer instead to help at the Battle of the Trench or the Battle of Ḥunayn lack evidence. The “word of the faithless” is not disbelief or idolatry in general, but the Meccan leaders’ decision in Dār al-Nadwa to kill the Prophet and end his mission. Allah’s “word” is His promise of assistance and victory. The verse thus recalls the plot to capture, kill, or expel the Prophet and declares that Allah thwarted that plot and fulfilled His promise.
verses.41:
Al-Mizan explains khifāfan and thiqālan as the plural forms of “light” and “heavy.” Here, going forth heavily means doing so despite impediments such as business, attachment to family, dislike of separation, or lack of provisions, transport, and weapons; going forth lightly denotes the opposite condition.

The command to go forth whether lightly or heavily therefore covers every ordinary condition and admits no excuse based on such obstacles. Similarly, striving with possessions and persons means using whatever means one has in Allah’s way. The command remains subject to genuine exemptions from jihād, such as illness, blindness, or lameness; these are not what “lightly or heavily” denotes.
verses.42:
Al-Mizan explains ʿaraḍan qarīban as a near, fleeting worldly gain, safaran qāṣidan as an easy journey that is not excessively long, and shuqqa as distance insofar as it causes hardship. The verse reproaches the hypocrites who stayed behind from the Prophet’s expedition to Tabūk, the distant campaign in which he personally took part and from which they held back.

Had there been easily obtained spoils or an easy journey, they would have followed willingly for worldly gain. But the great distance made the undertaking burdensome, so they remained behind. When reproached after the Prophet’s return, they would swear falsely that they would have gone had they been able. They destroy themselves either by preferring easy gain and inventing excuses when hardship arises, or specifically through their false oaths; Allah knows that they are liars.
verses.43:
Al-Mizan reads “May Allah excuse you!” as an invocation of divine pardon, comparable to other Qur’anic invocations, followed by a rhetorical question about the Prophet’s granting the hypocrites leave to remain behind. The apparent admonition does not rebuke the Prophet or charge him with sin. Rather, it exposes the hypocrites’ deceit: even the slight test of refusing them permission would have made the truthful and the liars manifest.

The address is indirect speech, directed to the Prophet so that the hypocrites’ wickedness becomes obvious. Saying that it would have been better not to grant leave means only that this would have better exposed them and that they deserved no such concession; it does not mean that compelling them to join the army was intrinsically better for the religion. Indeed, had they gone forth, they would have spread trouble, dissension, and division among the believers, supported by weak or diseased-hearted persons among the army who acted as their spies. Letting them remain behind was therefore the better protection for the army.

Their lack of preparation and their pleasure at staying behind already disclosed their hypocrisy and aversion to fighting. The Prophet, whose discernment was evident and whom Allah had repeatedly informed of their schemes, could recognize their hypocrisy and divisiveness, including from their manner of speech. He knew they would not truly wish to go forth whether or not leave was granted. By allowing them to stay behind, he preserved the appearance of their loyalty and Muslim unity; forcing their disloyalty into the open would have damaged the community’s morale, which was not yet inwardly united despite Islam’s outward strength.

Al-Mizan therefore rejects the claim that ʿafuww proves the Prophet committed even a minor sin, or that the question “Why did you do that?” necessarily implies wrongdoing. Such language can be rhetorical, including where a lesser matter is preferred to a greater one, though here the rebuke is not literal in the first place. Nor is the invocation a sign that the Prophet had committed a sin; it is divine grace and favour offered before any sin.

The commentary also rejects al-Rāzī’s view that the Prophet chose an inferior course through independent reasoning (ijtihād), and that prophets may err outside the conveyance of revelation, where ʿiṣma applies. Al-Rāzī cites the captives after Badr as another instance. Al-Mizan answers that the relevant verse criticizes the taking of captives, not their ransoming, and neither verse nor report establishes that the Prophet ordered captives to be taken. The accounts instead indicate that others pleaded for ransoms, seeking worldly wealth for the cause; the rebuke, “You desire the transitory gains of this world, while Allah desires the Hereafter” (8:67), is directed to the faithful. Reports making it a rebuke of the Prophet are mostly fabrications and interpolations. Moreover, the threat of great punishment in the following verse would indicate a major sin, not merely a loss of benefit, further showing that the censure was not directed at the Prophet.
verses.44:
Al-Mizan identifies seeking leave from jihād as a distinguishing mark of hypocrites. Genuine faith (īmān) in Allah and the Last Day entails striving in Allah’s way with one’s person and possessions and produces Godwariness (taqwā). The true believer, already Godwary before having faith in Allah and the Last Day, recognizes this duty and does not cling to the ground or seek exemption.

The hypocrite lacks true faith in Allah and the Last Day and so does not benefit from Godwariness. His heart is filled with doubt and hesitation; consequently, he prefers to avoid fighting and asks permission to remain behind.

verses.46:
Al-Mizan explains ʿudda as the supplies and equipment needed for an undertaking; inbiʿāth as hastening toward a goal; and tathbīṭ as detaining someone from an action by discouraging him. The verse confirms that the hypocrites lied when they claimed inability to go forth: had they truly wished to do so, they would have made the necessary preparations.

Allah’s aversion to arousing them was due to their hypocrisy, and was a benefit to the Prophet and the faithful, whom their presence would have exposed to dissension, discord, and disagreement. “Be seated with those who sit back” is not a legislative or moral command that conflicts with the command to go forth and fight. It describes what was said to the hypocrites because of their corrupt character, doubt-filled hearts, and desire to remain behind.

Allah does not directly attribute this instruction to Himself, thereby dissociating Himself from what displeases Him and suggesting agents such as Satan or the ego. Its indirect attribution shows it to be the consequence of the hypocrites’ own deeds, the benefit of their absence for the faithful, and the reconciliation of the command to go forth with the statement that they were told to sit with those who stay behind.
verses.47:
Al-Mizan explains khabāl as corruption and confusion, īḍāʿ as hastening to spread evil, and fitna here as tribulation through dissent and division. The hypocrites, had they joined the believers, would only have increased their disorder and hurried to sow sedition among them. Their aim was fitna within the community, and they had supporters or spies among the believers who were quick to listen and agree with them.

The verse explains why Allah was averse to arousing them in the preceding verse: their remaining behind was a blessing for the faithful. Its lack of an opening conjunction reflects this explanatory function.
verses.48:
Al-Mizan explains that the hypocrites had sought tribulation, dissent, and division before the campaign to Tabūk, as at Uḥud when ʿAbd Allāh b. Ubayy b. Salūl withdrew with a third of the army. They had upset the Prophet’s affairs by provoking disagreement, urging disobedience and desertion, encouraging Jewish tribes and idolaters to fight the faithful, and spying.

They continued these efforts until the truth that must be followed came and Allah’s command—the obligations of religion—prevailed, despite their aversion. The verse reinforces the preceding description of their conduct. It addresses the Prophet specifically because their efforts here were directed at upsetting his affairs, whereas the preceding verses concern their participation with the people.
verses.49:
Al-Mizan explains fitna as either a temptation that deceives a person or a general calamity. The hypocrites therefore ask leave to remain behind, either lest the prospect of spoils tempt them to join the expedition or lest going to battle subject them to tribulation.

Their request itself shows that they have already fallen into the fitna they claim to fear: disbelief, hypocrisy, and evil character have led them into Satan’s deception and straying. Thus they are encompassed by tribulation in this world, while Hell encompasses the faithless in the Hereafter. The wording may also mean that Hell already besieges them in this world, as indicated by the physical manifestation of a person’s deeds (tajassum al-aʿmāl).
verses.50: Al-Mizan holds that the good (ḥasana) and adversity (muṣība) in this verse are battle’s outcomes: victory and spoils, or death, injury, and defeat. The hypocrites are inwardly opposed to the Prophet: his success grieves them, but his misfortune makes them boast that they had protected themselves beforehand and depart exultantly. The following two verses provide God’s two answers to this attitude.
verses.51:
Al-Mizan explains that “He is our patron” establishes God’s exclusive governance of believers’ affairs: no apparent causes give them independent control, for every benefit, harm, good, and evil that reaches them has been ordained by God. Their task is to obey His commands and uphold His cause, while tawakkul means entrusting all affairs to Him.

The command that the faithful put their trust in Allah is consequently integral to the preceding statement, not an independent injunction. Since God alone cares for their affairs, believers should surrender their preferences concerning good and bad outcomes: good is His blessing, and adversity is also His will, so neither should produce exultation, grief, or reproach. Rejoicing at an enemy’s adversity or resenting an enemy’s prosperity is ignorance, since these outcomes are God’s affair. This is the first response to the hypocrites’ attitude.

The commentary rejects the view that mawlā here merely means “helper” and that the final clause is disconnected from the rest, since the context does not support it.
verses.52:
Al-Mizan identifies the two excellences (ḥusnayayn) with the preceding verse’s “good” and “adversity.” Although the hypocrites await either prosperity or misfortune for the Prophet and the faithful, both outcomes are good in Islam: victory brings worldly good and divine reward, while martyrdom or other hardship brings God’s pleasure and everlasting reward.

Thus the faithful await either victory and spoils or death in God’s path, and are content with either. By contrast, they await for the hypocrites either a direct punishment from God or punishment by the believers’ hands if commanded to fight them. This is the second response to the hypocrites: both sides wait, but every outcome awaited by the believers is good for them, whereas the outcomes they await for the hypocrites are punishment. The shift from the Prophet alone to the Prophet together with the faithful reflects their sharing, through following him, in whatever good or adversity reaches him.
verses.53: Al-Mizan explains the command to spend as conditional, not as an order: they are not forbidden to spend, willingly or under compulsion, but under no circumstances will it avail them or be accepted. The reason is their transgression, for God does not accept the deeds of transgressors and “Allah accepts only from the Godwary” (5:27).
verses.54: Al-Mizan explains that this verse details the transgression (fisq) that prevents the hypocrites’ charities from being accepted. Their pillars of hypocrisy are disbelief in Allah and His Messenger, laziness in prayer, and reluctance to spend in God’s way.
verses.55:
Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet is not to be impressed by the hypocrites’ abundant wealth and children. Though apparently desirable, these are not blessings leading to happiness, but a tribulation through which God punishes them in this life and causes their souls to depart with difficulty while they remain faithless.

Worldly life yields true happiness only when a person takes from it beneficial knowledge and righteous deeds without distraction by what brings no good. That is life under God’s patronage, free of the fear and grief that accompany death, hardship, and pain. But one deceived by worldly attractions, false promises, and remote hopes suffers through the very wealth and children thought to provide pleasure. The more worldly abundance turns such a person away from divine servanthood, the nearer he comes to destruction and spiritual torment; the world’s changing and contradictory means make his supposed ease a narrow and miserable life.

Straying from God’s remembrance thus immerses a person in temptations and hardships misidentified as blessings, until he disbelieves and abandons servanthood. God’s granting of wealth and respite is, in this case, His imperceptible drawing of the person into ruin, ending in death in faithlessness.
verses.56: Al-Mizan explains that the hypocrites swear that they belong with the believers, but are really a frightened people, anxiously expecting harm. If they could find a maljaʾ, a shelter from harm; maghārāt, a hiding-place such as a cave or mountain tunnel; or a muddakhkhal, a passage into which they could slip secretly, they would rush there with such frantic haste that nothing could hold them back.
