verses.58: Al-Mizan explains yalmizu-ka as blaming or reproaching the Prophet concerning charities. Their reproach arises when they are not given a share, whether because they have no entitlement to it or for other reasons; if given, they are pleased, and if denied, they are angry.
verses.59:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse rebukes people who received something from Allah and His Messenger but were not content to accept it. “Allah is sufficient for us” means that God suffices in what they seek and hope for, while “Allah will give to us out of His grace, and His Messenger” states what they desire, not a prediction of future provision.

They should have been content with what they received from the accumulated charities or elsewhere, seeking God’s grace and the Messenger’s giving while relying on God alone. The verse attributes giving to God and His Messenger, but confines sufficiency (kifāya), grace, and desire to God, in keeping with monotheism.
verses.60:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse specifies the eight exclusive causes for obligatory charities, as shown by “an ordinance from Allah”: the poor, the needy, charity administrators, those whose hearts are to be reconciled, slaves, debtors, expenditure in God’s way, and travellers. It responds to hypocrites who reproached the Prophet over charities by restricting their expenditure to these causes.

The poor (faqīr) and needy (miskīn) are distinct. A poor person lacks enough property to meet his needs, unlike the rich (ghanī). A needy person is poorer still: unable to meet his needs and reduced to a pitiable, humiliating condition, such as one forced to beg or labour in extreme deprivation, including the blind or lame. Every needy person is poor, but not every poor person is needy.

Those employed to collect charities gather and distribute them for the government. Those whose hearts are to be reconciled may receive a share to induce submission, fighting Islam’s enemies, or assistance in the religion’s needs. Spending “on slaves” means purchasing freedom, especially for a makātib unable to complete the agreed payment, or freeing a slave in difficulty. Debtors may receive funds to discharge their liabilities. “In the way of Allah” is a broad category encompassing every undertaking that benefits Islam, Muslims, or religion, most plainly striving in God’s way but also public-benefit works such as roads and aqueducts. The traveller (ibn al-sabīl) is one stranded far from home without means for the journey, even if prosperous at home.

The first four categories are introduced by li (“for”), while the latter four are apparently governed by fī (“on,” literally “in”). Al-Mizan takes li in the first group to signify ownership or the exclusive right to dispose of the funds. The verse thereby establishes the proper causes and excludes others, but does not itself settle jurisprudential questions about whether ownership is legally individual or collective, or how shares are apportioned; jurists disagree over these matters.

Several explanations have been offered for the shift in prepositions. One holds that the categories descend in priority, so the earlier causes are worthier, but this denotes priority of expenditure rather than a mandatory order of disbursement. Another, reported from al-Zamakhsharī in al-Kashshāf, treats fī as showing that the latter four are the worthiest recipients, with the repeated fī highlighting “in the way of Allah” and the traveller over slaves and debtors. It argues that these causes combine relieving poverty with freeing people from bondage, worship, or assistance to one separated from home. Al-Mizan objects that this conflicts with li in the first four categories, since an owner’s connection to property is stronger than a container’s connection to its contents.

A further view holds that li marks the first four as owners of the charity, whereas the latter four are beneficiaries for whose welfare funds are paid to others: for example, masters or sellers receive payment for freeing slaves, and creditors receive debtors’ shares. This is a sound explanation except for its somewhat overwrought treatment of the traveller, whom it includes under “in the way of Allah” while allowing the phrase to be linked instead to li. It would also be plausible to link debtors and travellers to li, while explaining fī for slaves and God’s way through the latter view.

“An ordinance from Allah, and Allah is all-knowing, all-wise” means that zakāt is an obligatory duty established by God’s knowledge and wisdom and not subject to alteration. More specifically, the context makes it most appropriate to understand the ordinance as the divinely fixed division of charities among these eight causes, so they may not be spent elsewhere. Consequently, “those whose hearts are to be reconciled” is not a category confined to particular nobles in the Prophet’s time or abolished after Islam’s triumph; the need to reconcile hearts did not disappear.
verses.61:
Al-Mizan explains that the hypocrites call the Prophet an “ear” (udhun) because he listens to what people say. “An ear of what is good for you” admits two readings: a listener to things good for them, such as revelation and believers’ advice; or, more aptly in context, an ear that is good for them. Under the latter reading, he hears even speech containing no good with respect and charitable interpretation, without assuming ill intent, shaming the speaker, or treating every report as an accurate account on which to act.

The latter interpretation is supported by “He has faith in Allah and has faith towards the faithful.” Īmān here means regarding someone as truthful. The Prophet believes the truth of God’s revelation; his faith towards the faithful, indicated by li rather than the explicitly object-marking bi in “faith in Allah,” means that he treats a reporter as believing his own report, without necessarily accepting the report’s content or acting upon it. Otherwise the Muslims’ affairs would fall into disorder. Even if alternative explanations of li—as merely making yuʾmin transitive, or adding the sense of inclination—are considered possible, they do not change this conclusion.

“The faithful” apparently means the community claiming faith, including hypocrites, while “those of you who have faith” denotes its genuinely faithful members. The Prophet respects each member’s outward profession without accusing him of lying, and this is mercy to true believers because it guides them to the straight path. If “those who have faith” instead denotes the earliest believers before the victory, it is an honorific usage, and “the faithful” likewise means those who truly believed in him.

The mercy in this verse is actualized mercy for those who truly believe: through him God saves them from error and secures their happy, noble fate. This differs from his potential mercy to all humankind in “We did not send you but as a mercy to all the nations” (21:107). He is a potential mercy for believers and unbelievers alike, present and future, because the religion and way of life brought through him transform society, restrain its deviation toward misery, and illuminate the path of fiṭra. Some have begun and will complete that path; others have left the path of misery without yet entering it, or desire to leave misery but have not yet done so. Islam’s spread and influence upon cultures and traditions manifest this wider mercy.
verses.62:
Al-Mizan, citing Majmaʿ al-Bayān, distinguishes aḥaqq from aṣlaḥ: aḥaqq can describe entitlement apart from human action, as when someone is worthier of property, whereas aṣlaḥ cannot. God is therefore aḥaqq of obedience, but not aṣlaḥ of it. Aṣlaḥ implies potentiality or receptivity, while aḥaqq conveys actuality and necessity; potentiality cannot be attributed to God, who is purely active and never passive.

The shift from addressing the Prophet to addressing the faithful draws attention to the principle that, if they are believers, Allah and His Messenger are more worthy of being pleased than the hypocrites are. True believers must please rather than oppose them, for opposition brings great disgrace and everlasting Hell.

The singular pronoun in “that they should please Him,” rather than a dual pronoun, is an etiquette of monotheism. Though God and another may be jointly mentioned with respect to some right or quality, God possesses His rights and qualities essentially, whereas others possess theirs only accidentally. The Qurʾan similarly distinguishes the Prophet when mentioning him together with the faithful.
verses.63:
Al-Mizan, citing Majmaʿ al-Bayān, explains muḥadda as striving to transgress the bounds: opposition, taking the opposite side, or hostility. Its root can mean preventing or detaining, and may also denote the impetuous loss of sound judgment that prevents right action; khizyu means lowliness and humiliation.

The verse’s rhetorical question expresses amazement and confirms that Allah and His Messenger are more worthy of being pleased. People know that opposing or angering them leads to eternal Hell, the great disgrace. Therefore, whoever believes in Allah and His Messenger is obliged to please them.
verses.64:
Al-Mizan explains that the hypocrites had repeatedly seen their concealed hypocrisy, blasphemous speech, mockery, and schemes disclosed to the Prophet in Qurʾanic verses. Although they did not believe the Qurʾan was revelation brought by Gabriel, they supposed that believers were spying on them and reporting to the Prophet, who then publicly exposed them. They therefore feared not revelation as such, but the exposure of their inner unbelief, designs against the Prophet, and efforts to thwart his mission by one of the Qurʾanic chapters he recited with divine authority.

The verse addresses the Prophet, who knows that this speech is truly divine revelation, and consequently calls it a chapter sent down by God, rather than describing it according to the hypocrites’ belief that it was human speech presented as revelation. Their apprehension was that the Prophet would recite a chapter unveiling their secrets before the people. The command, “Go on deriding,” is an ironical challenge exposing their incapacity: their derision is their hypocrisy itself—their outward profession of what they inwardly reject, as in, When they meet the faithful, they say, ‘W e believe,’ but when they are alone with their devils, they say, ‘W e are with you; we were only deriding’ (2:14). They may persist in concealing themselves, but God will uncover what is hidden in their hearts.

This interpretation resolves the apparent difference between their fear of a chapter being sent down and God’s bringing out what they fear: the object in both cases is the public disclosure of their hypocrisy. Al-Mizan rejects the proposed reading, “let the hypocrites be apprehensive,” because it lacks evidence and renders the end of the verse senseless. It also rejects the view that their apprehension was mock pretence: prior revelations had already exposed their secrets, so they had genuine grounds for alarm. Likewise, the common explanation that they merely doubted the Prophet’s truthfulness is inadequate. The verse uses ḥadhar, not merely khawf: ḥadhar denotes guarded apprehension and taking precautions against an anticipated harm, which implies experience of earlier disclosures and fear that they would recur, rather than bare uncertainty.

Nor does Al-Mizan accept that “against them” means merely “about them,” since this makes the following phrase, “informing them about what is in their hearts,” redundant. It also rejects referring “them” to the faithful. The wider discourse concerns the hypocrites and addresses the Prophet; the preceding address to the faithful is a temporary shift in address (iltifāt), not the governing context. Referring the pronoun to the faithful would introduce an unnecessary and rhetorically unsuitable ambiguity. The pronoun therefore refers to the hypocrites themselves. Revelation may be sent down “upon” them because it concerns their affairs, exposes their wrongdoing, and rebukes their hypocrisy; outwardly, they belong to the community of the faithful. The use of ʿalā also conveys the coming down of revelation from above, while its being sent to or upon a people means that it addresses what benefits them in this world and the next.

Finally, “deriding” cannot mean that their apprehension itself was insincere, since earlier Qurʾanic disclosures made their fear credible. It names the hypocrisy by which they professed with their tongues what they did not believe in their hearts. Thus God’s promise to bring out what they apprehend means that He will unveil their concealed two-facedness and inform people of the wicked contents of their hearts.
verses.65:
Al-Mizan notes, citing al-Ṭabriṣī and al-Rāghib, that khawḍ originally means entering and moving through water or mud, and came figuratively to mean delving into matters; the Qurʾan commonly uses it for blameworthy involvement. The hypocrites’ anticipated answer, “W e were just gossiping and amusing ourselves,” implies that the Prophet had found them engaged in conspicuous and suspicious conduct connected with him. Once questioned, they could offer no excuse except to portray it as idle jest rather than a serious act.

Their appeal to gossip and amusement was itself discreditable, especially for people professing faith and dealing with matters concerning God and His Messenger. It indicates both that their visible conduct was gravely suspect and that they used this excuse to conceal their real design. God therefore commands the Prophet to answer them on the basis of their own excuse: “Were you deriding Allah, His signs, and His apostles?” Their attempt to call their conduct jest is thus an admission of an even graver evil—mockery of God, His signs, and His Messenger—and is tantamount to disbelief.

From the surrounding indications, Al-Mizan concludes that they had devised harm against the Prophet, such as assassination or a deadly trap, had taken practical steps toward it, and held wicked discussions about it. Their plot failed and the Prophet was unharmed. When their conspiracy came to light, they dismissed it as gossip and amusement; God then rejected their excuse and disclosed their real intention. The verse may especially aim to show that their conduct mocked the Messenger. Since the Messenger is a sign of God, deriding him entails deriding God’s signs and, consequently, God Himself.
verses.66:
Al-Mizan explains that ṭāʾifa denotes a group or a portion of something and is not restricted to three or more persons; it can validly designate even one individual or two within a larger body. Those who deny this impose a numerical restriction unsupported by either usage or the word’s sense of a portion.

“Do not make excuses. You have disbelieved after your faith” rejects the hypocrites’ claim that their conduct was mere amusement: that excuse does not avert their disbelief. Here “faith” means their outward profession and appearance of faith, not the genuine divine guidance that is never followed by error. This is supported by (9:74), which speaks of their renouncing faith after their submission (islām), that is, after their outward utterance of the two testimonies. Faith can also exist at weak levels and be lost; the Qurʾan speaks of people believing and then disbelieving. But firmly rooted faith and established belief do not fade, for one whom God guides is rightly guided.

The conditional statement, “If We forgive a group among you, We will punish another group,” shows that the hypocrites in question were numerous and that punishment had become due against them collectively. If some are spared because a religious benefit or wisdom requires it, the punishment must fall upon others. Thus the connection is not that forgiveness of one group inherently causes punishment of another, but that a collective sentence remains to be executed even when some are exempted.

Accordingly, forgiveness (ʿafuww) here means sparing people worldly punishment for a religious or political expediency, not forgiving sins because they repented. Repentance is separately offered to all of them in (9:74); had the forgiveness here meant repentance, there would be no reason to punish any who repented. Both the sparing and the punishment in this verse concern this world, since punishment in the Hereafter is removed only through repentance or intercession, neither of which is at issue here.

The words may grammatically remain within the speech God commands the Prophet to address to them. Yet the apparent sense of what follows indicates a transition (iltifāt) in which God Himself directly addresses the hypocrites. This shift conveys the extremity of His wrath: rather than merely having His Messenger convey the threat, He confronts them with a punishment from which there is no refuge.
verses.67:
Al-Mizan holds that these verses do not merely begin a separate general description of hypocrites and believers. Rather, they explain the preceding statement that, if some hypocrites are spared, others will be punished. They are still addressed directly to the hypocrites and answer the question of whether such punishment would be guilt by association: hypocrites, men and women, are “from one another” because they share the same corrupt qualities, deeds, and consequent requital. Their common spiritual and moral character unites them despite their multiplicity. Mentioning women may emphasise this unity and perhaps indicate that women too participated in seditious groups and activities against the Muslim community.

Their shared traits are that they command evil, forbid good, and are tightfisted. They have forsaken God’s remembrance and the way of divine servanthood; hence God has “forgotten” them by withholding the reward granted to servants mindful of their Lord. The sequence shows that enjoining good, forbidding evil, and spending in God’s way are themselves forms of remembrance.

God includes the faithless with hypocrites because, before Him, they are alike in their final condition. Their promised recompense is the Fire of hell, in which they remain; it suffices them as their recompense. His curse means their banishment from mercy, and their punishment is lasting, without end or escape.

Al-Mizan explains khalāq as the share of blessings a person acquires through moral character. The verse continues the address to the hypocrites begun in (9:66) and compares them with earlier disbelievers and hypocrites in order to establish that all hypocrites, men and women, belong to one another. They share one nature: turning away from God’s remembrance, occupying themselves with transient worldly enjoyments such as wealth and children, and gossiping about God’s signs.

Those before them were stronger and possessed more wealth and children, yet their worldly share neither thwarted God nor saved their works from failure and loss in this world and the Hereafter. The present hypocrites have followed their course in enjoyment and vain talk, and so their works too will fail and they will be losers. The comparison intensifies the warning: if peoples more powerful and prosperous than them could not escape, the weaker hypocrites around the Prophet have still less reason to hope for escape.
verses.70:
Al-Mizan explains that God now turns back to address the Prophet, referring to the hypocrites as “them,” and recalls the fate of earlier peoples. The people of Noah were drowned; ʿAd, the people of Hūd, were destroyed by an earthquake; the people of Abraham, ruled by Nimrod, were deprived of divine blessings; and the overturned towns were those of the people of Lot, whose land was turned upside down.

Their messengers brought manifest proofs—clear signs, arguments, and evidence—yet they denied them and were destroyed. God did not wrong them: He had made truth and falsehood, sound judgment and deviation, and guidance and error clear. They wronged themselves by becoming immersed in worldly enjoyments, mocking God’s signs, and rejecting His messengers.
verses.71:
Al-Mizan presents this verse as the contrasting general description of the faithful. Faithful men and women, despite their differences of number and gender, share one undivided reality and are therefore comrades of one another. Their comradeship (wilāya) makes the members of the community look after one another, enjoin good, and forbid evil.

They maintain prayer and give zakāt, the two principal pillars of Islam: prayer embodies the relationship between God and His creation, while zakāt embodies relations among people. Obedience to Allah comprises all divine laws. Obedience to His Messenger includes the Prophet’s ordinances for governing and ordering communal affairs, including military commands, judicial judgments, and the application of criminal law; from another perspective, it also includes obedience to the divine law proclaimed by him.

God has ordained mercy for believers marked by these qualities, in contrast to the hypocrites whom He has forgotten. The closing words, “Indeed Allah is all-mighty, all-wise,” apparently explain this promise: nothing can obstruct His mercy, and His wisdom contains neither defect nor gap.
verses.72:
Al-Mizan explains that ʿAdn means abiding or dwelling in a place; thus the Gardens of Eden (jannāt ʿAdn) are gardens in which the faithful will dwell eternally. Along with everlasting gardens beneath which streams flow and good dwellings, God promises them something greater: His pleasure.

The indefiniteness of riḍwānun min Allāh magnifies it, indicating either that divine satisfaction cannot be measured or encompassed by human minds, or that even the smallest share of it outweighs all the delights mentioned. Its superiority is not merely that Paradise flows from God’s pleasure, though this is true, but that true divine servanthood is to serve God out of love for Him rather than desire for Paradise or fear of hell. For one who loves God, the greatest happiness is the pleasure of the Beloved, not the satisfaction of one’s own desires.

“That is the great success” conveys an exclusive sense: divine pleasure lies at the heart of every great success, even the attainment of Paradise. Without the reality of God’s pleasure in its blessings, Paradise itself would be a misfortune rather than a blessing.
verses.73:
Al-Mizan explains jihād or mujāhada as exerting one’s utmost to resist and repel a people, whether by word, deed, or fighting. Against open faithlessness, the command to strive means warfare, since the faithless openly oppose the Prophet. Against hypocrites, however, it cannot ordinarily mean fighting: they conceal their unbelief and hostility and work through plots and conspiracies.

The more plausible meaning is that the Prophet must exert whatever effort is expedient to resist them and frustrate their designs. Depending on circumstances, this may include isolating and avoiding them, verbally admonishing them, banishing them, or putting them to death when treason has been established. The command to be severe supports this broader meaning of striving, requiring harshness and forcefulness toward them. Their destination in hell perhaps supplies the reason they deserve such resistance.
verses.74:
Al-Mizan reads the verse in light of the hypocrites’ suspicious deed, their excuse that they had merely been gossiping and amusing themselves, and their subsequent oath that they had not said the offending words. God declares them liars in both respects: they did utter “the word of unfaith,” and their attempted deed was what they “contemplated” but failed to achieve. Their excuse of jest was therefore a denial of both their words and their real design.

The statement that they “renounced faith after their submission” (islām) shows that their words amounted to disbelief after embracing Islam. Al-Mizan suggests that the earlier wording, “You have disbelieved after your faith” (īmān) (9:66), may be the Prophet’s speech, judging them by their outward claim to faith, whereas this verse is God’s speech, judging their inward reality. They had only pronounced the two testimonies and were Muslims in outward submission, not true believers; their words explicitly rejected one or both testimonies and so annulled that submission. Alternatively, the earlier verse may concern their failed harmful deed, which damages faith but does not by itself alter a person’s outward Muslim status, while this verse concerns their spoken excuse, which does alter that status because it is determined by profession.

Their vindictiveness is especially blameworthy because Allah and His Messenger had enriched them through spoils, security, comfort, means of wealth, guidance to a righteous life, just distribution, and justice. What should have produced gratitude instead produced rancour, as if they treated divine kindness as cruelty and provision as a motive for denying God’s signs.

The pronoun in “out of His grace” refers to God. Al-Ṭabrisī, in Majmaʿ al-Bayān, reports that the dual pronoun is avoided out of reverence for God’s magnificence, and that all grace belongs to God while the Messenger is himself part of God’s grace. Al-Mizan adds that divine oneness is not numerical oneness, such that another could be added to God to form two, three, or any other number.

Despite their explicit faithlessness and failed conspiracy, repentance remains open to them and would bring forgiveness and Paradise. If they refuse it, they will suffer painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter. Worldly punishment may consist in making an example of them or in the Prophet being directed to plan their destruction; moreover, because hypocrisy opposes the causal order founded on fidelity and sincerity, that order itself turns against hypocrites, breaks them, and exposes them. Their punishment in the Hereafter is hell.

They will find neither guardian nor helper on earth to manage their affairs, avert punishment, or aid them in resisting it. United by corrupt beliefs, the hypocrites share a corrupt root that cuts them off from the means and resources to which they might otherwise have recourse.
verses.75: Al-Mizan explains that although ītāʾ, like iʿṭāʾ, means giving, it is usually associated with God’s grace (faḍl), whereas iʿṭāʾ is used for wealth. Here ītāʾ plainly means wealth, since those making the pledge promise charity from what God gives them, and the following verse concerns their stinginess. The context indicates an event that actually occurred, and narrations identify it with Thaʿlaba, though the verses’ general meaning remains clear: they pledged righteousness and charity if enriched, then begrudged God’s bounty and turned away.
verses.76: Al-Mizan explains that although ītāʾ, like iʿṭāʾ, means giving, it is usually associated with God’s grace (faḍl), whereas iʿṭāʾ is used for wealth. Here ītāʾ plainly means wealth, since those making the pledge promise charity from what God gives them, and the following verse concerns their stinginess. The context indicates an event that actually occurred, and narrations identify it with Thaʿlaba, though the verses’ general meaning remains clear: they pledged righteousness and charity if enriched, then begrudged God’s bounty and turned away.
verses.77:
Al-Mizan explains that aʿqaba means to bequeath or cause something to follow another, and can also signify recompense. The pronoun in “it caused hypocrisy to ensue” may refer to their stinginess: their miserly refusal to give charity implanted hypocrisy in their hearts, and they encounter its recompense. Alternatively, the pronouns may refer to God, so that He requited them by allowing hypocrisy to take root until they encounter Him.

The encounter may denote the Day of Judgement or the day of death, but the latter is more plausible, since it means that their stinginess endures until death rather than until resurrection, after which their condition cannot change. Their stinginess produced hypocrisy because it entailed breaking their promise to God and persisting in lies; both create the discrepancy between inward and outward states that defines hypocrisy.

The commentary concludes that breaking promises and lying are both causes and marks of hypocrisy. It also shows that hypocrisy can afflict one after belief, just as apostasy follows belief. Sin may lead to denial of God’s signs: when this denial is inward and outward it is disbelief, but when only inward it is hypocrisy. As God says, Then the fate of those who committed misdeeds was that they denied the signs of Allah and they used to deride them (30:10).
verses.78: Al-Mizan explains that najwā means hidden communications. The verse’s rhetorical question rebukes them by affirming that Allah knows their secrets, their secret talks, and all that is Unseen.
verses.79:
Al-Mizan explains that muṭawwiʿīn derives from taṭawwuʿ, doing what the soul neither dislikes nor finds difficult; it therefore commonly denotes supererogatory or recommended acts, unlike obligatory acts, whose abandonment the soul dislikes. Here the voluntary donors are wealthy faithful who can give charity without hardship, contrasted with poor people who possess only what their efforts have enabled them to acquire, or who struggle to be content with their small means.

The verse may begin a new discussion or, according to some commentators, further describe those who pledged themselves to Allah in (9:75). In either case, it condemns people who criticize and mock both prosperous donors and impoverished donors. Allah’s putting them to ridicule answers their mockery, and the painful punishment is a threat against them.
verses.80:
Al-Mizan explains that the juxtaposition of “plead forgiveness” and “do not plead forgiveness” shows that supplicating for these hypocrites and abstaining from it are equally pointless, like “spend willingly or unwillingly, it shall never be accepted from you (9:53).” They will never receive forgiveness, whether forgiveness is sought once, many times, or not at all.

“Seventy” signifies abundance rather than a literal limit. The obstacle is their defiance of Allah and His Messenger—that is, their disbelief—so no number of pleas can affect their state. The closing statement, “and Allah does not guide the transgressing lot,” completes the argument: having disbelieved, they are transgressors who have abandoned divine service; God does not guide such people; and forgiveness, being guidance to God’s proximity and Paradise, can never encompass them.
verses.81:
Al-Mizan explains that mukhallafūn are those left behind, maqʿad figuratively denotes their failure to go forth to fight, and faraḥ and surūr are states opposed to ghamm. Khilāf may mean disobedience, or possibly “after”; yet the wording khilāfa Rasūl Allāh, rather than addressing the Prophet directly, exposes their joy as disobedience to God, since the Messenger only conveys His revelation.

Their call, “Do not go forth in this heat,” was meant to discourage others and frustrate the Prophet’s mobilisation. The reply that hellfire is hotter means that fleeing worldly heat through refusal to fight casts them into the more severe heat of Hell. The use of law in should they understand (law yafqahūn) suggests that there is no hope of their understanding.
verses.82:
Al-Mizan relates the verse to those who rejoiced at evading their duty to strive. Their little laughter is their brief worldly exultation at remaining behind, whereas their abundant weeping is in the Hereafter amid the hotter fire of Hell. The imperatives express the necessary causal connection between their deeds and their requital, not a moral command to laugh and weep.

It is also possible that both imperatives concern this world and jointly constitute the requital of their deeds: their few days of illusory respite after disobeying the Messenger are followed by lasting humiliation before God and the faithful, as well as severe punishment in Hell in the next life.
verses.83:
Al-Mizan takes “the first time” to mean their original refusal to go forth when the Prophet commanded them, most likely in the campaign to Tabūk. They are therefore permanently barred from going out or fighting with him and told to remain with those who stay behind. This latter expression most naturally refers to those generally unable to fight—women, children, the sick, and the lame—though it has also been read as those who stay behind without excuse or as immoral people.

The words “If God brings you back to a group of them” indicate that this connected sequence of verses was revealed after the Messenger had set out and returned to Medina, during the time of Tabūk.
verses.84:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse forbids the Prophet and the faithful to perform funeral prayers for hypocrites or stand at their graves, because they disbelieved in God and His Messenger and died transgressors. Their disbelief and transgression likewise explain why seeking their forgiveness is futile, as stated in Whether you plead forgiveness for them or do not plead forgiveness for them… (9:80) and It is the same for them whether you plead for forgiveness for them, or do not plead for forgiveness for them: God will never forgive them. Indeed God does not guide the transgressing lot (63:6).

When faith is lost and the heart is consumed by disbelief, there is no room for salvation; thus praying for these hypocrites’ forgiveness or over their dead is pointless.
verses.85: Al-Mizan refers the meaning of this verse to its earlier commentary on so let not their wealth and children impress you… (9:55). Their possessions and children are not grounds for admiration, but means by which God punishes them in this world while their souls depart in faithlessness.
verses.86: Al-Mizan explains that ūlū al-ṭawl are those possessing power and blessings, while khawālif denotes those who stay behind. Despite their means, these people ask permission to remain behind when called to faith and striving with the Messenger; their satisfaction with this condition accompanies hearts sealed so that they do not understand.
verses.87: Al-Mizan explains that ūlū al-ṭawl are those possessing power and blessings, while khawālif denotes those who stay behind. Despite their means, these people ask permission to remain behind when called to faith and striving with the Messenger; their satisfaction with this condition accompanies hearts sealed so that they do not understand.
verses.88:
Al-Mizan contrasts the hypocrites with the Messenger and the believers who are truly faithful, rather than merely outward members of the community. Their striving with possessions and persons shows that they do not gladly remain behind and that their hearts are not sealed. They attain felicity in this world and a divine light of guidance.

“All the blessings” (al-khayrāt) encompasses every good that brings them nearer to their Lord, including a good life, divine guidance, and martyrdom. They are consequently the felicitous and successful ones.
verses.89:
Al-Mizan stresses that God has “prepared” gardens for these believers, rather than simply “promised” them them. The wording considers the outcomes of their deeds; a promise to particular people who believed alongside the Prophet would require Paradise for them even if they later changed and went astray, since God does not break His promises.

Such a guarantee conflicts with the Qurʾanic worldview and God-given human nature, for one past act cannot secure Paradise and forgiveness while leaving a person free thereafter to do as he wishes. Qurʾanic promises instead attach to general qualifying categories, such as faith and righteous deeds, which determine whether a person merits them; they are not guarantees to specified individuals, since that would contradict moral duty and knowledge of assured Paradise.
verses.90: Al-Mizan says it appears that the Bedouins who sought leave had genuine excuses, such as lacking provisions or weapons. Their contrast with those who lied to God and His Messenger supports this reading. Though genuinely unable to fight, they still came to request leave in response to the duty of striving and aiding God and His Messenger, whereas the hypocritical liars who stayed behind were wholly unaffected by that duty. The comparison exposes the hypocrites’ blameworthiness and moral and spiritual corruption.
verses.91:
Al-Mizan distinguishes the ḍuʿafāʾ, who are permanently unable to fight, from the marḍā, whose illness creates a temporary incapacity, and from those unable to provide the wealth, equipment, or resources needed to fight. They are excused from an obligation that would impose unbearable hardship, unlike those able to fulfil it who wilfully stay behind and merit blame and punishment.

This exemption depends on sincerity to God and His Messenger. The excused must be free of dishonesty and treachery and must not share the hypocrites’ purpose of undermining the Prophet’s mission, turning affairs against him, and corrupting the faithful; otherwise they share the hypocrites’ blame and punishment. Their sincerity makes them virtuous, and “There is no blaming the virtuous” supplies the reason for their security. Sabīl, literally “way,” indicates that no avenue of harm or penalty reaches them, and the statement appears to be a universal principle applied here.
verses.92:
Al-Mizan, citing al-Ṭabrisī, explains li-taḥmilahum as providing mounts such as horses or camels. Tafīḍ denotes overflowing, and ḥuzn is the heart’s pain at loss. Grammatically, there is no blame on the poor who came seeking a mount and necessary battle provisions, were told that none could be found, and turned back with eyes overflowing in tears because they lacked means to spend in God’s way and fight His enemies.

These tearful poor are not a fourth exempt category, but a particular group among those unable to spend. Their separate mention displays God’s special consideration, since they are even more sincere and virtuous than the others.
verses.93: Al-Mizan says blame belongs only to the well-off who seek leave to stay behind; pleased with those who stay back, God seals their hearts so they do not know.
verses.94:
Al-Mizan explains that the plural “you” addresses both the Prophet and the faithful. When the hypocrites offer excuses after the return, they are told not to do so because “we will never believe you” means that their excuses will not be believed; alternatively, it may mean they will not be believed in a manner favourable to them. God’s disclosure of their state explains this refusal.

Their hypocrisy and deceit are already known, God and His Messenger will observe their conduct, and they will finally return to the Knower of the sensible and the Unseen, who will inform them of the reality of what they did.
verses.95: Al-Mizan says that they are to be left alone when they swear and offer excuses, not because their oaths are accepted, but because they are filth and should be avoided. There is no need to expend effort rebuking them; Hell is their final refuge and the fitting requital for their deeds.
verses.96:
Al-Mizan explains that the hypocrites swear not only to escape rebuke but also to win the believers’ approval. Their oaths must be disregarded and they must be avoided, lest the purity and sanctity of faith be stained by their hypocrisy, deceit, faithlessness, and transgression. Even if believers are reconciled to them, God will never be reconciled to transgressors.

Thus reconciliation with them means being pleased with what displeases God. The verse subtly prohibits the faithful from ever being reconciled with the hypocrites.
verses.97: Al-Mizan explains that Aʿrāb, originally the plural of ʿArab, came to denote desert-dwellers; Aʿrābī means a desert-dweller, whereas ʿArabī denotes proper speech and iʿrāb explanation. The verse concerns these desert-dwellers, who are more severe in unbelief and hypocrisy because their distance from Medina and urban society deprives them of knowledge, morals, and other humanistic blessings. They are consequently more liable to ignorance of the limits of the teachings and ordinances God sent down to His Messenger, including religious duties, practices, and what is permitted and prohibited.
verses.98:
Al-Mizan explains maghram as a financial misfortune or obligation, from a root denoting something inescapable, and dawāʾir as circulating reversals, usually calamities. The Bedouins described here deem expenditure in God’s way a forfeiture and await a calamity that would free them from the believers’ authority and permit their return to idolatrous and erroneous customs.

What they spend may include expenditure for jihād and every good cause, and may particularly refer to charity. The latter reading appears supported by the following verse’s contrast—those who regard their spending as nearness to God—and by the later command concerning charity. Thus, certain desert-dwellers regard righteous expenditure or charity as a loss while awaiting misfortune for the believers; yet misfortune will fall upon them instead. This may be read either as a divine decree or an imprecation. God hears their speech and knows what their hearts contain.
verses.99: Al-Mizan holds that “the blessings of the Messenger” is joined to “what they spend,” so that “it” refers jointly to their expenditure and to the Messenger’s blessings. Some Bedouins sincerely believe in God’s oneness without associating partners with Him, and in the Last Day, accountability, and recompense. They therefore regard spending in God’s way, together with the Messenger’s prayers and blessings that it brings, as nearness to God. God promises to admit them into His mercy, for He forgives sins and is merciful to the faithful and obedient.
verses.100:
Al-Mizan notes that the standard recitation joins “the Helpers” to “the Emigrants,” yielding the early vanguard of both groups. Yaʿqūb’s alternative recitation, with a ḍamma on “the Helpers,” would extend the description to all the Helpers. Proposed identifications of al-sābiqūn al-awwalūn with those who prayed toward both Jerusalem and Mecca, attended Ḥudaybiyya, fought at Badr, or converted before the Emigration are not strongly supported by the verse’s wording.

The commentary instead holds that the expression denotes those distinguished by their early Emigration and fighting for the Prophet: those who first hastened to faith and laid the religion’s foundations before it became powerful. “Vanguard” and “followers” are relational terms, but awwalūn identifies the very first generation: those who believed before the Prophet’s migration to Medina, those who emigrated with him before Badr, and those in Medina who believed, sheltered, aided, and stood ready to defend him before Islam’s triumph. This includes emigrants who endured persecution and abandoned their homes and possessions for Ethiopia or Medina, and helpers who sheltered and defended the Prophet and the emigrants.

The verse establishes three classes among non-hypocritical believers until the Day of Judgement: the early vanguard of the Emigrants, the early vanguard of the Helpers, and all those who follow them in virtue. The first two are followed by others; the third class is unrestricted to a period or generation and is only “followed” in a relative sense by later people.

“In virtue” does not mean that the predecessors were virtuous and their followers merely imitated that virtue, nor simply that followers perform good deeds. Because iḥsān is indefinite, it specifies the virtuous manner of following: they follow the vanguard because the truth is with them, which is equivalent to following the truth itself, rather than following out of prejudice, desire, personal gain, or imitation detached from truth. Virtuous following also requires one’s conduct to correspond fully to what one follows. The alternative interpretation—following them while also doing righteous deeds—does not fit the Arabic; even if accepted, it would be included within following truth for its own sake, which entails good deeds but is not entailed by them.

The verse consequently praises the first two classes for priority in faith and in establishing and championing the religion, and gives them superiority over others. The min in “of the Emigrants and the Helpers” is partitive (tabʿīḍ), not explanatory (bayān): only some, not all, Emigrants and Helpers are the early vanguard. The Qurʾan itself speaks of Emigrants and Helpers with sickness in their hearts, as spies for hypocrites, as transgressors, or as persons whose conduct the Prophet repudiated; God cannot be pleased with transgressors.

Likewise, God’s pleasure, forgiveness, and promised gardens are contingent upon faith and righteous conduct. The surrounding context praises believers while condemning hypocrites, and Qurʾanic promises of reward for believers are consistently so qualified. Treating this verse as an unconditional guarantee of divine pleasure, forgiveness, and paradise for anyone called an Emigrant, Helper, or Follower would contradict such verses as God shall not be reconciled to the transgressing lot (9:96); and God does not guide the transgressing lot (9:80); and God does not like the wrongdoers (3:57), as well as the principle that whoever commits evil shall be requited for it (4:123). It would require qualifying numerous unqualified Qurʾanic warnings and teachings on recompense, undermining divine reward and punishment, religious ordinances, and the wisdom of revelation.

Al-riḍā, being pleased, means consenting without inward aversion. A servant is pleased with God when he neither dislikes what God wills nor loves what God detests; this requires submission to both God’s cosmic decree (qadāʾ) and His religious ordinances. Thus, the servants described are those who remain faithful and righteous, and God has prepared gardens for them.

God’s pleasure is an attribute of action (ṣifat al-fiʿl), not of essence (ṣifat al-dhāt). It means that He treats a person as one with whom He is pleased, admitting him to mercy and blessing him; displeasure means withholding mercy and subjecting him to tribulation. Otherwise, changes from obedience to disobedience or repentance would imply change in the Divine Essence. God may therefore be pleased with someone and later displeased, or the reverse. Yet in this verse His pleasure is apparently one after which there is no wrath, because it concerns the enduring character of the best believers, early and late, who have faith and do righteous deeds—not a temporally delimited group. This differs from God was certainly pleased with the faithful when they swore allegiance to you under the tree (48:18), where the pleasure is explicitly connected to a particular time and could be followed by displeasure.
verses.101:
Al-Mizan explains ḥawl, “around,” as adjacency on several sides, and maradū as persistent recalcitrance and evil practice. The verse therefore concerns hypocrites among the desert-dwelling Bedouins surrounding Medina and among Medina’s inhabitants, whose repeated hypocrisy has become habitual. Though the Prophet does not know them, God knows them; He will punish them twice and then consign them to a great punishment.

Commentators differ over the two punishments: capture, killing, or the like in this world followed by punishment in the grave; payment of zakāt followed by grave punishment; a penalty for treason followed by grave punishment; or exposure and disgrace followed by grave punishment. The verse itself supplies no evidence decisively establishing these interpretations, though the first is the most suitable if one must be chosen.
verses.102: Al-Mizan distinguishes these people from the hypocrites: they are sinners who confess their sins and mix righteous deeds with evil ones. The possibility that God may accept their repentance keeps them between hope and fear, preventing despair and abandonment of salvation. The ending, “Indeed God is all-forgiving, all-merciful,” particularly emphasizes hope.
verses.103:
Al-Mizan explains that tuṭahhir, “cleanse,” removes polluting dirt so that a thing is ready to grow and display its blessings, whereas tuzakkī, “purify,” makes it grow and flourish by bringing out its goodness. The verse deliberately joins cleansing with this productive purification.

“Take charity from their possessions” commands the Prophet to collect charity from people’s wealth. The plural amwāl indicates that it is taken from diverse forms of property: gold and silver; camels, cows, and sheep; and wheat, barley, dates, and grapes. “To cleanse them and purify them thereby” is addressed to the Prophet, not an adverb qualifying charity: by taking charity from these forms of wealth, he cleanses and purifies the payers.

To “bless them” is to pray for blessing upon both them and their property, as the Prophet used to invoke blessing for those who paid zakāt. Such prayers are a sakan, a source of rest, security, and trust for them, and express gratitude for their effort in God’s way. The conclusion, “God is all-hearing, all-knowing,” likewise comforts zakāt-payers. By its apparent meaning, the verse legislates zakāt on property, one of Islam’s pillars, as numerous traditions from the Imams of the Prophet’s Household and others explain.
verses.104:
Al-Mizan takes the question as an exhortation to give zakāt willingly and eagerly. Charity is truly given to God, while the Messenger or tax collector receives it on His behalf; in this sense, the recipient is God. The verse thus encourages servants to deal directly with their Lord, as though their hands touched His when they give, while God remains wholly free of physicality and transcendent above time and space.

The association of charity with repentance rests on the fact that both purify. Paying charity is a kind of financial repentance, while repentance is a kind of charity performed through one’s deeds and movements. God’s names the All-clement and the All-merciful encompass both acts. Giving charity and paying zakāt are therefore forms of repentance.
verses.105:
Al-Mizan says that although this verse follows the command concerning charity and may particularly encourage the faithful to give it, its wording is general: it includes everyone who acts, whether believer, hypocrite, or disbeliever. At minimum, it addresses believers and hypocrites together.

The verse resembles (9:94), where God and His Messenger observe the hypocrites’ conduct. The two passages suggest that God knew the concealed aims of the hypocrites and made them known to the Messenger through revelation. In the present verse, the true character, aims, effects, and benefits of the faithful’s deeds—including Godwariness, reform of Islamic society, aid to the needy, and the purification and increase of wealth—are known to God and His Messenger, and are witnessed by the faithful among themselves.

The faithful mentioned cannot merely be ordinary believers who observe the outward effects of deeds. Such effects eventually appear for every people, and believers and hypocrites alike inhabit the same society; this would not explain why believers are singled out as witnesses, or why they do not similarly witness the hypocrites’ deeds. The phrase “and you will be returned to the Knower of the sensible and the Unseen” distinguishes the present world from the Resurrection. Before the Resurrection, people see only the outward appearance of their own deeds; on the Day of Judgement God will inform them of their realities. Yet God, His Messenger, and “the faithful” see the conduct in this world. Since God can disclose the realities of deeds to His Prophet, “the faithful” here means those believers who are witnesses to deeds, not the whole body of believers, as in Thus W e have made you a middle nation that you may be witnesses to the people, and that the M essenger may be a witness to you (2:143).

The verse thus means: people may perform whatever good or evil deeds they wish, but God sees their realities; His Messenger and the faithful who witness deeds also see them in this world; and, on the Day of Judgement, the doers will return to the Knower of the sensible and the Unseen and be shown their deeds’ true reality. Its purpose is to make people watchful over their conduct: no deed is veiled from God and those whom He has made witnesses, and God will remove the veil from the doers themselves on the Day of Judgement, as in You were certainly oblivious of this. W e have removed your veil from you, and so your sight is acute today (50:22). A deed performed before observers differs greatly from one thought to be hidden.

By contrast, (9:94) addresses particular hypocrites who offered excuses after Tabūk. God commands the Prophet to reject those excuses because revelation had informed him and the faithful accompanying him of their conduct. That verse says that God and His Messenger observe the hypocrites’ deeds and that God will reveal their reality to the hypocrites on the Day of Resurrection, but it does not mention the faithful as witnesses. This is the essential difference from (9:105). A more literal alternative remains possible: God may mention only Himself and His Messenger to the hypocrites because their plotting was against God and His Messenger, while mentioning the faithful when addressing everyone encourages righteous action in the company of the righteous without concern for disbelievers’ and hypocrites’ opinions.
verses.106:
Al-Mizan explains that those “awaiting God’s edict” stand neither nearer to punishment nor to forgiveness; their affair rests entirely with whatever God wills. Read independently, the verse appears to concern the abased in the land (mustaḍʿafīn), who occupy an intermediate position between the virtuous and the wicked.

Reports concerning the occasion of revelation say it concerned three men who remained behind from Tabūk, later repented, and whose repentance God disclosed to the Messenger. Nevertheless, the verse itself does not state their ultimate outcome. Its conclusion, invoking God as the All-knowing and All-wise, remains deliberately indeterminate: God will judge them according to His knowledge and wisdom. This contrasts with the preceding verse, whose ending—“Maybe God will accept their repentance. Indeed God is all-forgiving, all-merciful.”—more directly gives hope of repentance’s acceptance.
verses.107:
Al-Mizan explains ḍirār as causing harm and irṣād as taking a place from which to lie in wait and observe. The opening wa may, if these verses were revealed with the preceding ones, enumerate yet another group of hypocrites; if revealed separately, it begins a sentence whose subject is those who built the mosque and whose predicate is “Do not stand in it ever!” (9:108). Other grammatical analyses are omitted as overly tortuous.

The mosque was built by hypocrites to harm others, divide the faithful, and serve as an ambush point for enemies of God and His Messenger. This accords with the reported account: after the Banū ʿAmr b. ʿAwf built the mosque at Qubā and the Prophet prayed there, envious hypocrites of Banū Ghanim b. ʿAwf built a neighboring mosque to undermine it and divide its congregation. They awaited the Christian monk Abū ʿĀmir, who had promised to bring a Roman army to expel the Prophet from Medina and instructed them to prepare for fighting.

While preparing to march to Tabūk, the Prophet was asked to pray in their mosque and invoke blessing there; he promised to do so after his return, when the verse was revealed. Thus, their claimed wish to provide another place of worship was deceit: God testifies that, despite their coming oath that they intended only good, they are liars.
verses.108:
Al-Mizan explains that God first forbids the Prophet ever to pray in the hypocrites’ mosque, then directs him to the mosque of Qubā, which was founded from its first day on Godwariness and is therefore worthier for prayer. Its superiority rests on the pure intention of its founders, unlike that of the hypocrites’ mosque.

Although “worthier” alone does not necessarily make prayer at Qubā obligatory, the preceding absolute prohibition on praying in the other mosque conveys this requirement. “Therein are men who love to keep pure,” followed by “God loves those who keep pure,” identifies the mosque as Qubā rather than the Prophet’s Mosque or another mosque. Its people love to purify themselves from sins or impurities, and God loves such people; hence the Prophet should pray among them.

“A mosque founded on Godwariness” explains why one mosque is better than the other, while “Therein are men who love to keep pure” explains the superiority of one congregation over the other. The opening of the following verse, “Is he who founds his building on Godwariness” (9:109), further explains why the people of Qubā surpass the hypocrites who built the Mosque of Sabotage.
verses.109:
Al-Mizan explains the image of one who builds on “the brink (shafā) of a collapsing bank (jurufihārin)” as a metaphor. Shafā is an edge, juruf a stream-eroded valley bank, and hār, derived from hāʾir, denotes collapse through inherent softness. The hypocrites resemble one who builds at an unstable water’s edge: his building falls into the valley and takes him with it, the valley signifying hell. This contrasts with one who founds his building on Godwariness and God’s pleasure—that is, who orders his life around protection from God’s punishment and the attainment of His satisfaction.

It appears from the context that the two foundations represent the respective religions and ways of life of believers and hypocrites. The believer’s religion rests on certainty about God, Godwariness, and seeking His pleasure; the hypocrite’s rests on doubt and hesitation. Therefore, the hypocrites’ building remains a disquiet, or source of doubt, in their hearts, which never reach certainty, until their hearts are cut to pieces and their doubts are shattered with them. God, all-knowing and all-wise, thus lowers one group and raises the other.

verses.111: Al-Mizan explains ishtarā as purchasing a commodity by paying its seller. God portrays His binding promise of paradise to those who strive in His way with their persons and possessions as a contract of sale: God is the buyer, the faithful are the sellers, their lives and possessions are the commodity, paradise is the price, and the Torah, Evangel, and Qurʾan are the receipts. This subtle metaphor grounds God’s congratulation to the faithful on their bargain and their great success.
verses.112:
Al-Mizan takes the verse to mean that the faithful are characterized by these lofty qualities. Individually, they turn from all other than God towards Him, devote themselves to worship, praise and magnify Him, travel to places where He is remembered and worshipped, and bow and prostrate in prayer. Collectively, they enjoin religious good and forbid evil. Preserving God’s bounds (ḥudūd) joins their individual and communal life: it means not merely avoiding transgression, but attentively guarding those bounds in public and private.

The order is deliberate: individual qualities come first, then the communal duty of enjoining good and forbidding evil, and finally the quality that embraces both spheres. Siyāḥa means travel to sites of God’s remembrance and worship, such as mosques—not fasting, travel to contemplate earlier peoples’ ruins, travel to acquire knowledge, or travel to collect Prophetic sayings. The latter meanings may be supported by other verses, but they lack a basis here and would disrupt the verse’s arrangement of attributes.

Through these qualities, faith (īmān) is completed and the believer becomes entitled to God’s guarantee of paradise. The glad tidings given by both God and His Messenger emphasize that, having observed God’s rights, they will receive what God has undertaken to grant them.
verses.113:
Al-Mizan holds that once it is clear that polytheists are destined for hell, it is clear that they are enemies of God; the Prophet and the faithful then have no right to seek their forgiveness, even if they are relatives. Such a prayer is pointless, and the humility required of a servant of God precludes invoking Him for what cannot avail. The wording denies them a right that divine law would need to establish for the act to be permissible.

The commentary distinguishes a servant whom God detests because of a fault or sin from a servant who is God’s enemy through wilful, defiant opposition. Mercy and forgiveness may be sought for the former if he is humble and not recalcitrant. Intercession and prayers cannot benefit the latter unless he repents, abandons arrogance and obstinacy, and submits humbly; forgiveness and generosity are meaningless for one too arrogant to receive them.

Abraham sought forgiveness for his idolatrous father only in fulfilment of his promise, because he did not yet know him to be an obstinate enemy of God. When this became manifest and it was clear that he would not abandon idolatry and error, Abraham repudiated him. His forbearance made him endure his father’s harshness and promise to pray for him; his plaintiveness (awwāh) denotes deep grief arising from fear and longing for his Lord, and he grieved over his father’s idolatry.

verses.115:
Al-Mizan reads these verses as the rationale for forbidding prayers for the idolaters’ forgiveness. Having received guidance, the faithful risk being led astray if they do not avoid what God has made them aware they must avoid: here, treating idolaters who are God’s enemies with prayers for forgiveness or affection. Like the principle that God does not change a blessing bestowed on a people until they change what is in themselves (8:53), the verse shows that God continues guidance and blessings until people alter themselves through ingratitude or transgression, whereupon He deprives them of these gifts.

God’s exclusive kingdom over heaven and earth, and His power to give life and death, establish that He alone is the real guardian and helper. The faithful must therefore disassociate themselves from God’s enemies, take no guardian except God and those among His chosen friends whom He permits, and not exceed this limit by taking His enemies as guardians.

The principle is general: one must disassociate from God’s enemies and may not take them as allies or guardians, whether by seeking forgiveness for them or otherwise. It applies to idolaters, disbelievers, hypocrites, innovators, deniers of God’s signs, and those persisting in major sins, such as usury or making war on God and His Messenger.

verses.117:
Al-Mizan explains sāʿat al-ʿusra as a period of hardship, such as thirst, hunger, or extreme heat. Yazīgh, “to swerve,” means departing from truth; in this context, hearts nearly swerved by becoming sluggish in answering the Prophet’s call to arms or in taking a difficult route home. According to Majmaʿ al-bayān, khullifū means falling behind those who have gone ahead, rather than leaving something in a place; bi mā raḥubat refers to the earth’s expanse despite its felt narrowness.

The two verses concern distinct situations but form one connected revelation. God turned clemently to the Prophet, the Emigrants, and the Helpers who followed him in hardship, even though some hearts nearly swerved; and He turned clemently to the three left behind after their sin. The repeated tawba moves from the general clemency shown to all mentioned to its particular application to each group. Perhaps the chief purpose is to console the three, restore them fully to the community of the faithful, and efface the effects of their sin, placing them with the others among those to whom God has turned mercifully. The Prophet himself was neither sinful nor near to swerving: the verse praises the Emigrants and Helpers for following him, and his prior mention ennobles him.

The Emigrants and Helpers followed the Prophet during the campaign to Tabūk despite severe hardship and the near wavering of some among them. The three left behind were crushed by isolation, since people, even their families, would not speak to them; grief weighed on them until they knew that there was no refuge from God except in Him through penitence. Al-Mizan understands God’s inclusion of the Prophet as showing that mercy toward the Prophet’s community is part of His mercy toward the Prophet: the Prophet is the intermediary through whom goodness and blessings descend upon his community, and God mentions him first when honourably mentioning those with him.

In thumma tāba ʿalayhim in both verses, tawba means that God returned to them by granting guidance and success. A servant’s repentance is encompassed by two divine acts of tawba: first, God grants guidance and success so that the servant seeks forgiveness; then He accepts that repentance and forgives. The first sense is required for the Emigrants and Helpers, who are not described as sinful, and is also required for the three, since God turned to them “so that they might be penitent” (li-yatūbū): He guided them to repentance before accepting it. The divine names al-raʾūf and al-raḥīm likewise support this reading rather than explicitly signifying acceptance of repentance.

The pronoun in li-yatūbū refers to the three left behind: God turned to them so that they might repent, after which He would accept their repentance and forgive them. Although the verse itself does not explicitly state that their repentance was accepted, despite the well-established traditional account that it was, its context and tone strongly suggest forgiveness. The general declaration that God turned clemently, the closing names All-clement and All-merciful, and their recognition that refuge lies only in Him make it unthinkable that God would reject those whom He guided to seek refuge through repentance; compare, acceptance of repentance by God is only for those who commit evil out of ignorance, then repent promptly. It is such whose repentance God will accept, and God is all-knowing, all-wise (4:17).

The commentary rejects as nonsensical the claim that God merely made repentance easy so that they might repent, the literal rendering that li-yatūbū means returning to their state before sin, and the claim that its pronoun refers instead to all the faithful. Finally, ẓannū in “they knew” means knowledge rather than mere thought because of the context.

verses.119:
Al-Mizan defines truthfulness (ṣidq) primarily as correspondence between a statement and external reality. Since beliefs and decisions may also be conceived as statements, a truthful person (ṣādiq) is one whose deeds conform to his beliefs and who fulfils what he resolves.

Because the command to be Godwary, the reference to the truthful, and the command to be with them are all general, “the Truthful” does not designate a particular group. To be with them means to follow their example in words and deeds. The verse thus commands the faithful to be Godwary and to follow the truthful; it does not directly command them to become truthful, for then it would have said, “be of the truthful.”
verses.120:
Al-Mizan explains that raghba with fī means desiring something for its benefit, while with ʿan it means aversion or neglect. In wa lā yarghabū bi-anfusihim ʿan nafsihi, bi indicates the cause of such aversion: concern for their own lives must not make the people of Madinah and the surrounding Bedouins indifferent to the Prophet’s life, so that they abandon him amid the dangers of war or the hardships of travel in order to enjoy worldly ease.

They have no right to hang back behind him. Every thirst, fatigue, or hunger endured in God’s way, and every step that enrages the faithless or secures a gain against an enemy, is written as a righteous deed. These acts make them virtuous, and God does not squander the reward of the virtuous.
verses.121:
Al-Mizan explains that every expense, whether small or great, and every valley crossed in God’s way is written to the believers’ account, so that God may reward them with the best recompense in the Hereafter.

God’s rewarding them “by the best of what they used to do” may be meant to motivate them most strongly, to imply recompense for all their good deeds through mention of the best, or to identify striving in God’s way as their best deed because it is most difficult and underlies Islam’s call. It may also mean that the recompense is the deed itself as it returns to God: the best deeds are literally the best reward. Further, God may forgive the sins that contaminate good deeds and conceal their defects, leaving only their best deeds for recompense. These latter two meanings may ultimately be one.
verses.122:
Al-Mizan reads “go forth en masse” as all the faithful going out to fight in God’s way, while the group from each section goes forth to the Prophet to become learned in religion. The faithful outside Medina may not all go to fight; each group should instead send a delegation to receive religious instruction while others fight.

Most fittingly, “when they return to them” means that those who have learned the religion return to their own people. It is also possible that it means their people return from fighting to the learned group after the latter have returned home. In either case, the learned delegation is to practise what it has received and warn its people by conveying the teachings and the harmful consequences of contravening them, so that they become Godwary and pious.

Yatafaqqahū fī al-dīn encompasses all the roots and branches of faith, not merely practical law as fiqh is commonly understood, since warning a people requires knowledge of all aspects of religion. The verse also lifts the obligation of fighting from students of religious knowledge. Other interpretations—such as all going to the Prophet to study, or a fighting group going forth while those remaining behind learn and warn them upon their return—conflict with the verse’s context.
verses.123:
Al-Mizan understands this as a general ordinance for fighting in God’s way that aims to expand Islam’s borders until they encompass the whole world: each group of believers fights the faithless in its vicinity, leading to the extension of Islam’s rule over all the earth and its inhabitants.

That the faithless should find “severity” in the believers means steadfastness for God’s sake, not coarseness, viciousness, evil character, or hardness of heart; such traits are condemned by Islam’s moral teaching, and verses on fighting prohibit transgression and viciousness. God’s being with the Godwary is a conditional promise of support: believers must remain vigilant over themselves and mindful that their Lord is with them, and that they have the advantage so long as they remain devoted to Him.
verses.124:
Al-Mizan explains that the question, “Which of you did it increase in faith?”, betrays hypocrisy. Its asker is inwardly unmoved by Qurʾanic revelation, finding neither fear of God nor love of truth but doubt and misgiving; he seeks others who will likewise deny its effect, so that he may justify his doubt and persist in hypocrisy.

The verse distinguishes healthy believing hearts from hearts diseased by doubt and hypocrisy. A newly revealed chapter increases believers’ faith because its divine guidance illuminates hearts already certain of their religion. This increase is both qualitative, as they receive further Qurʾanic teachings and realities, and quantitative, as those realities strengthen faith; hence they rejoice. For those whose hearts are sick, however, revelation adds defilement—that is, further error—to their existing defilement. Their contrast with believers shows that they possess no genuine faith, only doubt and obstinate denial, and thus die faithless. The Qurʾan consequently affects every hearer according to the condition of his heart: it increases healthy hearts in faith and joy, and diseased hearts in error and defilement.

verses.126: Al-Mizan takes the rhetorical question as an affirmation and rebuke: though they are tested at least once or twice each year, they neither reflect, repent, nor take admonition. Were they to consider these recurring trials, they would recognize what their state requires; instead, their continued disobedience brings further tribulation, increasing defilement, and finally permanent ruin and everlasting loss.
verses.127:
Al-Mizan identifies this as another mark of the hypocrites. When a Qurʾanic chapter is revealed, they exchange fearful, distressed glances because they cannot bear what they hear and fear that the concealed state of their hearts will be exposed. “Is anybody observing you?” (hal yarākum min aḥad) expresses the meaning of these glances rather than necessarily words they actually utter; min in min aḥad emphasizes that they fear observation by anybody at all.

They then slip away from the Prophet. In context, God’s turning aside their hearts means turning them away from understanding the revealed words of truth and from attaining genuine faith, because they do not understand. The phrase may also be read as an invocation, “May God turn aside their hearts!”; if so, it forewarns them of coming harm.
verses.128:
Al-Mizan identifies the messenger as the Prophet Muḥammad. Mā ʿanittum, “what distresses you,” derives from ʿanat, meaning destruction and harm. That he is “from among yourselves” apparently means that he is a human being of the same species as his audience, not that the address is restricted to Arabs or Quraysh.

The Prophet is grieved by people’s hardship and deeply concerned for them whether or not they yet believe, while being especially kind and merciful to the faithful. These qualities call people to obey him, since he proclaims only what God has commanded and obedience to him is obedience to God; they should recognize, honour, answer, and heed him. The verse’s descriptions are thus meant to induce people to listen to and accept his preaching, as the following verse’s mention of those who turn away further indicates.
verses.129:
Al-Mizan explains that if people reject the Prophet’s teaching, he is commanded to say, “God is sufficient for me. There is no god except Him.” God alone suffices, since there is no sufficer other than Him; alternatively, “There is no god except Him” may simply magnify His grandeur.

“In Him I have put my trust” conveys exclusive reliance on God and explains what divine sufficiency entails. Tawakkul is to take one’s Lord as trustee over one’s affairs, rather than rely on outward means, which cannot independently produce the desired result. It is reliance on the one true cause to which all other causes return. “He is the Lord of the Great Throne” accordingly signifies that all authority and sovereignty belong to Him and that He governs every affair.

By directing the Prophet to declare God’s sufficiency rather than merely command him to trust, the verse teaches trust with awareness of these realities. One should employ the means God has made available, while placing hope and trust in God alone to bring about the intended end. It also shows the Prophet’s deep concern to guide humankind to abiding, everlasting success.
